title: Look Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Efficient Diffusion VLMs

details.title: Look Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Efficient Diffusion VLMs
details.abstract: LOWN (Look Only When Needed) is a training-free decoding method for diffusion vision-language models (DVLMs) that processes the image only when a text-only prediction disagrees with the last image-conditioned prediction. Diffusion VLMs such as LLaDA-V process the whole image at every denoising step, but we find that removing the image changes a token being unmasked at only 22.8% of steps on average. Agreement certifies the earlier prediction for reuse, and the number of certified tokens sets how many are unmasked in that step. Without training or a tuned threshold, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V's score on ten benchmarks at 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs and cuts generation time by 57.4% on average. title: WorkFactory: Turning Professional Intents into Executable Work for Scalable Agent Training

details.title: WorkFactory: Turning Professional Intents into Executable Work for Scalable Agent Training
details.abstract: Excited to share WorkFactory, a scalable framework for synthesizing coherent and executable professional tasks to train Working Agents! WorkFactory combines professional intent synthesis, information support graphs, and execution-guided repair to construct high-quality tasks that enable reliable expert demonstrations. We build 112,686 tasks spanning 612 occupations and train the WorkPilot model family at 4B, 27B, and 35B-A3B scales. All three models achieve consistent improvements across four professional-work benchmarks, with WorkPilot-35B-A3B improving from 879 to 1565 Elo on GDPval-AA v2.1. We hope this work contributes to scaling general-purpose agents for real-world professional tasks!

title: A Broader Look into MLLM's Retrieval Heads

details.title: A Broader Look into MLLM's Retrieval Heads
details.abstract: We study how omni-modal LLMs retrieve relevant evidence, focusing on how retrieval mechanisms extend from text and vision to audio-visual inputs. Across 18 model checkpoints, including eight omni-modal models, we find that retrieval relies on a sparse set of attention heads that are largely preserved from language or vision-language backbones. By presenting the same evidence as speech or on-screen text, we show that audio and visual retrieval largely recruit the same heads. Ablating the shared subset, comprising fewer than 2% of all attention heads, also degrades document understanding, spatial perception, and visual mathematics, revealing its role in broader multimodal capabilities. Building on these findings, we optimize retrieval-head attention with a ranking objective for document retrieval, improving Qwen3-VL-8B’s page Recall@1 on MMDocIR by 6.03 percentage points over the untrained scorer, with gains across three model families.

details.title: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers
details.abstract: We introduce SpecSlot, a role-coupled tokenization method for pixel-space generative Transformers. SpecSlot decouples fine visual detail from global communication by assigning tokens fixed spectral output roles: low-frequency carriers perform global attention, while the remaining slots interact locally. On ImageNet-512, SpecSlot-K4 uses 38.2% fewer FLOPs than JiT-B/16. For 256×256 text-to-image generation, it reduces forward compute from 218.77 to 129.86 GFLOPs while improving DPG-Bench from 61.15 to 62.21. details.abstract: Excited to share VibeGame, a framework that turns prompts (text and optional reference images) into complete, playable 2D game projects! To let agents build a complete, vivid game with no given assets, we build an AI-native game engine that agents can read and control frame by frame. On top of it, a self-evolving team of eight agents designs the game, creates its own art and animations, writes the code, and plays and reviews the result until it passes. On 30 GameCraft-Bench tasks, VibeGame outperforms the strongest baseline harness by 11.70 points with GPT-5.6-Luna and by 4.19 points with GPT-6.1-Sol.

title: Co-Design Bench: Multimodal Collaborative Coding Evaluation for Agentic Models

details.title: Co-Design Bench: Multimodal Collaborative Coding Evaluation for Agentic Models
details.abstract: Can a coding agent turn a real user's multimodal request into a complete, working application revision? We're sharing Co-Design Bench: Multimodal Collaborative Coding Evaluation for Agentic Models , a benchmark built around real users' requests to revise existing applications. Each task starts with a runnable application and asks the agent to understand the user's intent, make the necessary changes, and satisfy every acceptance criterion. Real requests, multimodal inputs, and connected changes. Co-Design Bench contains 273 tasks and 2,331 expert-authored acceptance criteria , curated from 37,463 deduplicated queries across 26,314 real user coding sessions . It covers two complementary tracks: Multimodal Editing (100 tasks): localized revisions grounded in annotated screenshots and optional image, audio, video, or document inputs. Repository Editing (173 tasks): coordinated changes across components, routes, state, data flow, and content. Requests can involve reproducing distinct text animations from a video, correcting a dashboard from a receipt and updating its dependent totals, or coordinating layout and interaction changes across an application. Tasks span Grounded Understanding, UI Transformation, and Functional Implementation , often combining several capabilities within one request. Evaluate the running application, with evidence for each requirement. Our reference-free judge-then-refute protocol assesses hidden acceptance criteria using source code and browser evidence. A separate verifier challenges positive judgments for stubs, hardcoded outputs, unreachable functionality, and requirement mismatches. Evidence audits require screenshots for visual claims and recorded browser actions for interaction claims. No gold implementation or target screenshot is required. Partial requirement satisfaction and complete delivery tell different stories. Across 10 model endpoints under a shared agentic harness , the strongest endpoint, gpt-6-astra , passes an average of 69.9% of criteria per task , yet fully satisfies only 26.4% of tasks . All ten endpoints achieve lower criterion completion on repository requests spanning three or four edit types than on those spanning one or two. Qwen3.8-27B reaches 64.4% overall strict completion , ranking fourth overall, and 64.5% on Repository Editing , ranking second on that track in this evaluation. It also leads the text-only Multimodal Editing subset at 77.9% . Rankings vary with the editing setting; the small repository-track score differences do not establish a general model advantage. The ME-96 subset comprises 96 Multimodal Editing tasks and 521 acceptance criteria , a distinct scope from the full 273-task paper evaluation. Explore the real cases, demonstrations, evaluation tools, and results: Project & demos · Paper · Code & evaluation · Dataset We welcome researchers and builders working on coding agents, multimodal grounding, and reliable application editing to try the benchmark and share their findings!

title: Intrinsic Distribution Matching

details.title: Intrinsic Distribution Matching
details.abstract: Hi everyone! We’re excited to share IDM: Intrinsic Distribution Matching . Can a generator provide both the score supervision and the representation used for distribution matching? Building on internal DMD, IDM retains the full DMD correction and adds an explicit loss on the means and per-coordinate standard deviations of the generator’s own EMA features , without an external feature encoder. A Gaussian-plus-residual decomposition of the reverse-KL field motivates this additional moment constraint. At 2 NFE , IDM (Z-Image) achieves 94.25% on LongText-CN and 90.20% on LongText-EN , the best scores among the compared methods at this budget. Controlled ablations show consistent gains from the added moment loss, while generator EMA features perform competitively with DINOv2. We evaluate both Z-Image-Turbo 6B and Qwen-Image 20B with full-parameter and LoRA tuning. Model weights: coming soon. If you find the work interesting, we’d appreciate a GitHub star ⭐ and an HF upvote!

title: Investor's Last Exam: Can AI Agents Do Equity Investment Without Seeing the Future?

details.title: Investor's Last Exam: Can AI Agents Do Equity Investment Without Seeing the Future?
details.abstract: Evaluating forecasting capability usually means waiting for outcomes to materialize — months, sometimes years — during which market conditions, fundamentals, and the information environment shift enough that scores can no longer be cleanly attributed to the model; moreover, most work in LLM4Finance has focused on the research stage rather than the investment stage, which is where the field's core objective lies. ILE asks whether an agent, using only what was visible at decision time, can independently complete the full chain from evidence to assumptions to forecast. To answer it, we built a versioned corpus (3.43M document versions, 1.52TB, 9 source classes) that enforces the cutoff across the entire toolchain — specify a timestamp and you get exactly the versions visible at that moment — and organized 86 assignments around buy-side analyst deliverables, with rubrics anchored to sources and reproducible calculations through financial dependency graphs. Among current SOTA systems, Astra scores 78.9 on Research & Evidence but only 52.5 on Forecast & Model, and ordering by realized outcomes puts DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ahead (40.3 vs 37.7): today's models are very good at organizing evidence of what has already happened into coherent analysis, and not yet good at turning that analysis into judgment about what has not. For me, the longer-term significance is on the training side — once the time boundary is a mechanism, historical timestamps become a re-samplable environment for large-scale domain RL, with evaluation and training sharing one environment.

title: Glance: The Generator Is Its Own Reranker

details.title: Glance: The Generator Is Its Own Reranker
details.abstract: Glance: one model. Judge, rank, generate. RAG usually serves two models: a cross-encoder reranker that encodes every (query, passage) pair, then a generator that reads the winners again. We show the generator can be its own reranker. All k passages are prefilled once into a shared state, one short probe per passage continues from that cache, and a LoRA + pointer head scores every passage in the same pass. With the adapter off, the same weights chat as usual. On a 9B hybrid (Gated DeltaNet) backbone: 39 min of training on one B200: SciFact nDCG@10 0.741, NFCorpus 0.345 (bge-reranker-v2-m3: 0.721 / 0.326) Scales to k=200 candidates: 0.717 vs 0.659 for BGE (SciFact subset) HotpotQA answer F1 +0.045 over BGE-selected context, same generator (paired bootstrap CI excludes 0) Activated variant: chat stays bit-identical to the base model, and the answer continues the reranking cache Adapters + code (Apache-2.0): https://huggingface.co/airun-ai/GlanceRAG-MiMo-9B-Reranker

title: AskStream: When and What to Ask Proactively under Uncertainty in Streaming Video Understanding

details.title: AskStream: When and What to Ask Proactively under Uncertainty in Streaming Video Understanding
details.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models have increased interest in interaction paradigms for video understanding. The evolution from offline to streaming and proactive interaction has gradually shifted models from passive responders toward more proactive agents that can decide when to answer. However, existing proactive paradigms typically assume that the information required to answer a query is complete, leaving models to only wait or answer. In the real world, however, information is often incomplete due to uncertainty from either the video or the user. In proactive paradigms, such uncertainty can cause the model to wait forever or generate highly hallucinatory responses. We therefore argue that proactive interaction should be redefined with a third action: ask, allowing models to actively ask for missing information. To study when and what models should ask before answering, we introduce AskStream, the first multi-turn benchmark spanning video and user uncertainty for streaming video understanding, with four task categories and eight subtasks. It contains 438 videos with 2,714 manually annotated frame-level time windows across three types: wait, ask, and answer. Across both multiple-choice and open-ended settings, even the strongest model attains only 52.18% on our proposed Ask-F1 metric, highlighting substantial limitations in proactive information seeking under uncertainty.

title: Online Dense Reinforcement Learning with Planning-Grounding Agent for UI Navigation on Live IOS Apps

details.title: Online Dense Reinforcement Learning with Planning-Grounding Agent for UI Navigation on Live IOS Apps
details.abstract: While frontier vision-language models demonstrate strong capabilities in user interface (UI) navigation, their high inference costs prohibit everyday use. Conversely, smaller models trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or offline reinforcement learning often memorize static trajectories, leading to brittle execution and an inability to recover from errors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel online reinforcement learning framework that trains UI navigation agents directly on live iOS applications. Our framework decouples the agent into two specialized components: a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model. We rely on an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide comprehensive reward signals, combining dense, step-level feedback to evaluate intermediate progress with a terminal reward for overall task completion. To effectively leverage this dual reward structure, we optimize the agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with step-level advantage estimation. Furthermore, we introduce GiGPPO, a novel neighbor-conditioned value estimation method that improves critic stability by leveraging reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories. To support this online training paradigm at scale, we introduce an efficient infrastructure that orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices. Evaluations on rigorous benchmarks, including UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld, demonstrate that our online RL trained agents substantially outperform both SFT and terminal-only RL baselines while accelerating training convergence. Notably, our 8B RL agents achieve nearly a sevenfold improvement over the SFT baseline in out-of-distribution generalization to Android environments, while outperforming Gemini-3.5-Flash and tying with Gemini-3.1-Pro on real iOS applications.

title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm

details.title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm
details.abstract: Foundation models are typically trained in stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL), with changes in both data and learning algorithms. We show that this algorithmic separation is not fundamental. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, we place all of these stages under a single likelihood-based training algorithm, unified training. This perspective turns the foundation-model training lifecycle into a problem of choosing which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case. We instantiate this framework in a unified training system that mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer. Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning. This work lays the groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training, connecting mathematical principles, training infrastructure, and the development of model capabilities.

title: Your LR Schedule May Not Be Principled: Effective Learning Rate Scheduling in Weight-Normalized Training

details.title: Your LR Schedule May Not Be Principled: Effective Learning Rate Scheduling in Weight-Normalized Training
details.abstract: Weight-normalized (WN) training is emerging as a compelling alternative to conventional weight decay (WD), with recent studies reporting substantial pretraining loss gains. We show that these gains are driven primarily by the induced effective learning rate (ELR) trajectory rather than by normalization alone. Matching ELR trajectories largely collapses the training loss dynamics of WN and WD. Schedule design should therefore target ELR rather than the nominal learning rate (LR) alone. Building on this principle, we propose AIR ( A ffine I nverse-square- R oot decay), which combines a theoretically derived $1/\sqrt{t}$ decay with an affine adjustment to satisfy prescribed peak and terminal LRs over a finite training horizon. We further identify late-stage ELR scheduling as a key source of its gains, because a shared late schedule attenuates the effect of earlier LR choices. Experiments on 128 B-token Mixture-of-Experts pretraining demonstrate that AIR outperforms cosine and other candidate schedules in training loss, downstream performance, and hyperparameter robustness, reducing terminal training loss by approximately 0.01 relative to cosine at matched cumulative LR. Applying the same ELR trajectory to WD reproduces the corresponding training dynamics, showing that the benefits extend beyond fixed-norm training and establishing ELR as the principled scheduling object.

title: Scaling Lean Theorem Proving for Real-World Code Verification

details.title: Scaling Lean Theorem Proving for Real-World Code Verification
details.abstract: We present EasyProver, a Lean proving system built from recursive agents with isolated contexts, asynchronous search, parallel tactic probing, and an elastic elaboration service. Using an off-the-shelf frontier model with no additional training, it proves 669/672 PutnamBench problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations and resolves 597/600 NTP4VC verification conditions and all 189 VERINA tasks by proof or refutation. Because these benchmarks are close to saturation, we also introduce Aegis, which converts competitive programming problems into much harder verification tasks over real implementations. The pipeline writes safe Rust solutions, translates them into Lean with Aeneas, generates specifications, and labels each frozen statement with a kernel-checked proof or refutation. It produces 2,045 differentially validated Rust-Lean program pairs and 11,533 candidate specifications. Unlike hand-written benchmarks, these tasks carry implementation-level obligations from fixed-width arithmetic, explicit failure, generated loops, casts, and functionalized mutation. On a stratified sample of 2,000 statements, EasyProver proves 1,054 (52.7%) within a 30-minute budget per statement. The same tasks can also be used to benchmark other provers and as rewards for reinforcement learning.

title: Unlocking Any-Order Generation in Pretrained Autoregressive Image Models

details.title: Unlocking Any-Order Generation in Pretrained Autoregressive Image Models
details.abstract: Many AI image generators build a picture one piece at a time, always in the same order: left to right, top to bottom, like reading a page. Because of this fixed habit, they cannot fill a missing patch in the middle of a photo, extend an image beyond its borders, or redraw one region while keeping the rest. Existing alternatives are trained from scratch, at roughly three times the computing cost. We show that existing generators can instead learn to work in any order with brief extra training. Two ideas make this possible: the model is told which spot it will fill next, and training shifts gradually from the familiar order to random ones, so the model keeps what it already knows. The adapted models fill, extend, and edit images competitively, with a small loss in everyday image quality, letting today's models gain new skills without being rebuilt.

title: After One-Click Video: The Inflow of Service-Type Content, the Failure of the Recommendation Pool Mechanism, and the BoLe System

details.title: After One-Click Video: The Inflow of Service-Type Content, the Failure of the Recommendation Pool Mechanism, and the BoLe System
details.abstract: One-click video tools now let anyone make good-looking content fast. Most of it is service-type content: people watch it to meet a need, not to enjoy the content itself. Before competing, creators, tool builders and model researchers should first ask which kind they are making, because the two kinds win by different rules. Our paper draws this line, and uses a simple model to show why the free platform’s trial-viewing pool stops working when service-type content keeps pouring in. Try the demo: set AI output to 100x and watch one year.

title: FDSML: Formula-Driven Supervised Metric Learning with Parameter-Aware Triplet Loss

details.title: FDSML: Formula-Driven Supervised Metric Learning with Parameter-Aware Triplet Loss
details.abstract: FDSML pre-trains vision models without real images, using the generating formula itself as supervision: fractals with more similar parameters should lie closer in the embedding space. We turn this parameter-space ordering into triplets, so the model learns how images relate to each other.

title: R^2Orch: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Orchestration via Self-Play within a Skill-Internalization Loop

details.title: R^2Orch: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Orchestration via Self-Play within a Skill-Internalization Loop
details.abstract: R²Orch (Recursive Self-Play Orchestration) trains an agent orchestrator without a hand-designed curriculum: an inner self-play loop improves the orchestrator on tasks a Proposer picks, and an outer loop improves how that inner loop learns. The Proposer is rewarded for tasks whose rollouts keep reaching different outcomes as skills are withdrawn (Recursive Learnability), and each skill is withdrawn once self-play shows the orchestrator does as well without it (Skill Withdrawal), moving it toward zero-skill deployment. Tested with zero skills, a 9B orchestrator is best on all twelve benchmarks across QA, math, code, and interactive tasks, raising the average over the strongest baseline from 86.0 to 89.8 in distribution and from 76.1 to 78.8 out of distribution (AIME 2026: 74.0 → 81.3). title: Does Scaling Toward AGI Depend on What System-1 Lets System-2 Execute?

details.title: Does Scaling Toward AGI Depend on What System-1 Lets System-2 Execute?
details.abstract: Progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) has largely relied on scaling a resource-intensive executive, System-2, through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning, and more agents. We ask whether the next stage may come instead from co-designing it with System-1, a lightweight, semantically aware predictor that evaluates candidate interactions before execution, so that System-2 acts only on those worth their cost. Our answer is a qualified yes. We study conditional interaction, a predict--gate--execute--update loop: System-1 estimates each candidate's utility, System-2 executes those admitted by an adaptive threshold, and the outcomes update System-1. The loop spans training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and agentic tool use, with utility and cost defined by the application. Under ideal screening and equal execution costs, execution compute falls by a factor approaching $1/\rho_u$, where $\rho_u$ is the density of utility-relevant interactions (cost-weighted when costs differ); prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift reduce the saving. We bound selection regret by predictor error and the utility margin. These results motivate our central hypothesis: $\rho_u$ is a measurable coordinate of scaling efficiency and makes informative compute a better description of scaling than total compute.

title: FrameForge: Harnessing Priors of Video Foundation Models for Unified Image Generation

details.title: FrameForge: Harnessing Priors of Video Foundation Models for Unified Image Generation
details.abstract: Unified conditional image generation requires a single model to preserve different aspects of a visual input while producing a target image that follows textual guidance. Pretrained video models provide a promising foundation by encoding visual transformations across time, yet existing approaches typically assign the condition and target to fixed temporal positions. We observe that condition-target relationships vary substantially across generation tasks, while video models naturally encode visual transformations at different temporal scales. This motivates us to model conditional generation through input-adaptive virtual temporal relations. We propose FrameForge, which captures two complementary aspects of such relations. Mixture of Temporal Experts (MoTE) models how far the target lies from the condition by dynamically selecting temporal RoPE experts with different virtual intervals. Chain of Temporal Reasoning (CoTR) models how the condition is transformed into the target through a latent intermediate state, with a reasoning-bottleneck attention mask encouraging information propagation through this pathway. Experiments on DreamBench, COCO2017, and GEdit-Bench show that FrameForge achieves superior performance in subject-driven generation, canny-to-image generation, and image editing among the compared methods.

title: Wizard: Manipulate Any World in Real Time via Agentic Control

details.title: Wizard: Manipulate Any World in Real Time via Agentic Control
details.abstract: 🪄 Wizard: Manipulate Any World in Real Time via Agentic Control! Existing game world models produce realistic visuals but remain constrained by familiar environments and predefined motions. Control largely focuses on locomotion, with limited support for articulated actions. Can a world model follow an unseen character swinging a sword, spreading its wings, or transforming mid-battle? Wizard decouples character animation, scene manipulation, and gameplay logic from visual generation. Agents control articulated skeletons and scene geometry through structured visual proxies, while explicit world states support adaptive boss behavior and mechanics-consistent combat. We construct 50.3 hours of aligned proxy–video pairs spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters. Character-aware adaptive masking preserves reference appearance, while causal adaptation and few-step distillation enable interaction at 24 FPS, with zero-shot generalization to unseen scenes, characters, and motions. From world exploration and character summoning to transformation and scene manipulation, Wizard gives players greater freedom to create and control their own game worlds. Code coming soon!

title: HiFOR: Hierarchical Foresight with Action-Guided World Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Model

details.title: HiFOR: Hierarchical Foresight with Action-Guided World Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Model
details.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated promising capabilities in robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Recent advances have further incorporated future prediction to enhance the understanding of environmental dynamics and task progression. However, existing methods often model short-term dynamics and long-term task objectives separately, while directly incorporating predicted futures into action policies without sufficiently considering their relevance to current action requirements. To address these limitations, we propose HiFOR, a hierarchical foresight framework with action-guided world retrieval. Specifically, Hierarchical Foresight Prediction jointly predicts short-term state evolution, semantic milestones, and final goal states through a Hierarchical Dependency Mask (HDM), establishing dependencies across temporal horizons. Building upon these predictions, Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling organizes future latent representations along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions to facilitate fine-grained retrieval. Furthermore, Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval adaptively retrieves relevant future information from the structured latent world based on evolving action representations during denoising, providing targeted guidance for action generation. Extensive experiments on two simulation benchmarks and six real-world robotic manipulation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

title: CEPO: A General Framework for Improving Prompt Optimization in Multi-Agent Systems

details.title: CEPO: A General Framework for Improving Prompt Optimization in Multi-Agent Systems
details.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) require both effective coordination and specialized task execution. Existing prompt optimization approaches typically couple these functions within agent-specific prompts. We introduce Coordinator-Executor Prompt Optimization (CEPO), a general framework for improving prompt optimization in MAS. CEPO separates system-level coordination from agent-level execution through a shared coordinator prompt and agent-specific executor prompts, and guides their updates according to their respective roles. This structure allows shared coordination rules to be refined consistently across agents while keeping execution instructions separately adjustable. CEPO provides the prompt structure and optimization guidance, while existing prompt optimizers perform the underlying search. Extensive experiments spanning 11 benchmarks across four domains demonstrate that applying CEPO to four existing prompt optimizers consistently improves their performance. Ablations and qualitative analyses support the proposed design, while controlled studies on a document-understanding MAS further demonstrate improved optimization budget efficiency and performance scaling with the number of agents.

title: CaPtain: A Pipeline for Post-Training Code-as-Policy Robot Agents

details.title: CaPtain: A Pipeline for Post-Training Code-as-Policy Robot Agents
details.abstract: Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it. Code-aspolicy (CaP) puts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply. Yet, existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that brings this recipe to CaP and turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware. Within this harness, we first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, and then apply multi-turn RL. Multi-turn RL, however, must credit tens of requests from the agent, whose physical effects often surface several turns later, with a single outcome observed only at the end of the episode. Since training runs in simulation, we introduce a physical critic that reads the privileged physical state in simulator, which the policy never sees, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success. Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B achieves 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points). Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. We release all code, data, and model weights.

title: GLOW-FM: Efficient Generative Low-Light Image Enhancement with One-Step Latent Flow Matching

details.title: GLOW-FM: Efficient Generative Low-Light Image Enhancement with One-Step Latent Flow Matching
details.abstract: GLOW-FM:  Generative low-light image enhancement using Flow Matching. GLOW-FM combines a lightweight Tiny-VAE encoder with an Hourglass Diffusion Transformer (HDiT) architecture to perform efficient enhancement in a compact latent space. Trained with Terminal Velocity Matching (TVM), the HDiT restores low-light latents in a single step. Together, the compact architecture and single-step inference enable efficient generative low-light image enhancement.

title: HALO: Human-Grounded Granular Evaluation of Proactive Agents

details.title: HALO: Human-Grounded Granular Evaluation of Proactive Agents
details.abstract: Proactive agents must decide whether, when, and how far to assist without an explicit request. Existing evaluations often rely on automated scores or binary verdicts, offering limited human diagnosis of evidence use and intervention quality. To address these gaps, we introduce HALO, Human-Grounded GrAnular EvaLuation of PrOactive Agents. HALO-Arena covers 4 proactive need types, Dependency, Blockage, Risk, and Opportunity, across 10 everyday domains and 50 personal environments. Scenarios require agents to retrieve evidence from structured databases or unstructured documents before judging whether assistance is warranted and choosing its scope. On HALO-Arena, we construct HALO-8K, a dataset of 8,000 responses from 10 models across 400 scenarios, annotated by 20 experts for action level, acceptability verdicts, and human diagnosis. For rejected responses, human diagnosis covers timing, intensity, and other issues. Recorded reasoning tokens and retrieval rounds measure the effort behind these responses. The best proprietary and open-source models achieve 72.88% and 56.63% acceptability, respectively. Our central finding is that over-proactivity is the dominant observed failure mode, with Premature timing or Excessive intensity accounting for 61.20% of rejected responses. Further analyses yield complementary findings on the balance between intervention and restraint, evidence acquisition, and the calibration of timing and intensity.

title: WeFair: Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in Short-Video Search

details.title: WeFair: Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in Short-Video Search
details.abstract: Personalization should clarify user intent, not overwrite it. How can we build a compact query rewriter that understands users' personalized intent while avoiding intent drift? We introduce WeFair , a fidelity-aware alignment framework for personalized query rewriting in short-video search. The key idea is to align different types of human feedback with different stages of training: Demonstration (SFT): Learn from large-scale search-session data and real user reformulations. Preference (DPO): Capture user preferences from subsequent consumption behavior. Verification (GRPO): Use exact human reformulations and preservation targets to enforce intent fidelity. One of our key findings is that richer behavioral rewards do not necessarily lead to more faithful rewriting. Strict, verifiable human feedback proves more effective for preventing intent drift during on-policy optimization. Results are encouraging: WeFair-2B outperforms strong baselines in offline overall accuracy and intent preservation. Online A/B testing achieves a +2.593% relative lift in effective video-view rate and a 2.350% relative reduction in query reformulation rate . The model is deployed in WeChat short-video search, serving 100M+ queries per day . We hope this work offers useful insights into building efficient, reliable, and intent-faithful language models for real-world search systems. 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16927v2

title: On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning

details.title: On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning
details.abstract: We split the training-inference mismatch in LLM RL into a numerical discrepancy, which stays nearly constant, and a policy lag, which compounds through the trainer's own updates. From this split we derive the discrepancy-lag correction (DLC), which keeps stale-sampler training within the noise of on-policy runs.

title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory

details.title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
details.abstract: RoboArchitect automatically designs and continually improves a robotic agent around a frozen robot policy, without updating any weights. These agents develop their own control routines. Most converge on a dynamic split between the VLA policy and code-as-policy, and nearly all build a persistent memory across episodes. Average success rises substantially on unseen scenes and tasks. RoboArchitect also manages to evolve a unified agent across different robot platforms. title: Supervising the Visible State: Separating Representation from View Selection in Streaming Video

details.title: Supervising the Visible State: Separating Representation from View Selection in Streaming Video
details.abstract: An action seen once and the same action seen three times receive the same action-recognition label, so that supervision does not require a model to count. Answers shared across histories that differ in event order, accumulation, or relations leave those distinctions unconstrained; we call this state under-specification. Visible-State Supervision (ViSS) addresses it by training on source-grounded probes of event identity, order, accumulation, relation change, and answer sufficiency; under the same recent-frame interface it improves OVO-Bench over a strict-matched generic temporal supervision baseline while remaining comparable on StreamingBench, with the largest gain in hallucination detection. Test-Time Causal View Search (TVS) then adapts evidence access while keeping the learned model fixed, expanding from recent frames to sparse event and compact history views on demand. The two interventions separate representation from view selection: supervision particularly benefits hallucination detection and causal reasoning, access particularly benefits event recall and forward reasoning. Together they reach the best reported accuracy among the published systems compared here on StreamingBench and OVO-Bench at a fraction of the processed frames of exhaustive selection, and strict replay shows that most of the remaining gap to a three-view oracle is a correct answer that was later replaced. Streaming accuracy depends on what supervision asks the model to keep, what evidence inference exposes, and whether the model keeps a correct answer once it has one.

title: MemSteer: Turning User Histories into Supervision for Agent Memory Optimization

details.title: MemSteer: Turning User Histories into Supervision for Agent Memory Optimization
details.abstract: 🧠 You set a deadline by email, then moved it in chat. Which date will your AI assistant remember? We built MemSteer at Peking University and Microsoft Research Asia to turn a user’s own history into tests for agent memory. It connects facts across records, writes a question that requires putting them together, and keeps it only if a second reader can independently recover the answer and cite the evidence. When the agent gets a question wrong, MemSteer-Opt uses that evidence to trace the failure and test changes to how the agent stores, retrieves, and presents information. No hand-labeled questions or model fine-tuning required. 🔍 On ATM-Bench , MemSteer-Opt took a BM25 baseline from 54.9 to 68.3 in Question Score. The same optimizer reached 67.3 using official benchmark QA. 📬 On RHELM , accuracy improved over BM25 by 4.1 points with chats alone and 6.6 points when emails and documents were included. 📄 Read the paper

details.title: No Channels Left Behind: Understanding Diffusion Acceleration through Residual Gates
details.abstract: We find that REPA and dispersive regularization substantially reorganize AdaLN-Zero residual gates in diffusion transformers, suggesting that training acceleration arises partly from reshaping the residual gating pathway. Broader gate participation accompanies better generation quality across settings. Guided by this insight, we propose a teacher-free radial objective using feature-norm regularization, without pairwise comparisons. On ImageNet 256×256 with SiT-B/2, it improves FID over dispersive loss.

title: SciGame: Let Agents Play the Scientific Discovery Games in the Real and Counterfactual World

details.title: SciGame: Let Agents Play the Scientific Discovery Games in the Real and Counterfactual World
details.abstract: SciGame separates scientific law discovery from memorization. Every relation becomes a "scientific card" generating two worlds behind one interface: an Original environment following the published law, and a Counterfactual twin with a mutated but dimensionally consistent law. Memory passes the first and fails the second; only evidence gets through both. Agents run hypotheses, experiments and forecasts, scored on held-out prediction, strict success and explanation quality. Notably: strict success on Historical counterfactuals is 0% for all five Codex models tested, adaptive experimenting helps some models and hurts others, and ~48% of one model's failures show a near-perfect explanation with no symbolic equation ever written.

title: TernScope: Model-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient Ternary Endoscopic Segmentation

details.title: TernScope: Model-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient Ternary Endoscopic Segmentation
details.abstract: Hi everyone! I'm the first author of TernScope. Can a tiny segmentation network use ternary weights throughout—including the input and prediction layers—and translate that into smaller hardware? We co-design an endoscopic segmentation model and a matching accelerator: • 0.2483M parameters and 0.0949 GMACs at 256×256. • All 25 convolutions use ternary weights {−1, 0, +1} and 8-bit activations, trained through branch fusion and progressive QAT. • External evaluation on ClinicDB and ColonDB without fine-tuning. • 88.46% lower compute-array area than original INT8 Gemmini under matched 45 nm synthesis. Code, a W2A8 checkpoint, and accelerator RTL are available: https://github.com/ReaganWu/TernScope Happy to discuss full-network ternary quantization, efficient medical vision, and model–hardware co-design!

title: SketchDirector: Complex Scene Sketching via Agentic Layout Reasoning and Detail Refinement

details.title: SketchDirector: Complex Scene Sketching via Agentic Layout Reasoning and Detail Refinement
details.abstract: Existing sketch generation methods often rely on image guidance and are largely limited to individual objects or simplified scenes, leaving text-guided complex scene sketching underexplored. We present SketchDirector, an agentic framework that mimics the human sketching workflow for automatic multi-concept scene sketching. Given a scene-level text prompt, SketchDirector first employs a large language model~(LLM) to decompose the scene into multiple draft assets, where each is represented by a set of Bézier curves. Then, an agentic reasoning loop iteratively plans and executes their spatial arrangement, guided by self-evolving memory. Finally, a detail refinement module leverages diffusion priors to enhance sketch quality while preserving geometric structure. To support future research and applications in multi-concept scene sketch generation, we further introduce the \textit{MCSketch8K} dataset, comprising editable vector assets, compositional layouts, and object-level manipulation annotations. Extensive experiments show that SketchDirector outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in semantic and compositional quality while effectively preserving overall contour organization during refinement

title: TurnTurk-GPT: Text-Based Turn-Taking Prediction for Turkish

details.title: TurnTurk-GPT: Text-Based Turn-Taking Prediction for Turkish
details.abstract: This paper presents TurnTurk-GPT, a text-based turn-taking predictor for Turkish obtained by fine-tuning a Turkish GPT-2 model with the TurnGPT objective on synthetic and real dialogue, and evaluates it on real Turkish conversation against rule baselines, a zero-shot Turkish language model and a widely used multilingual end-of-turn detector. Evaluation uses word-level decision points on unpunctuated, lower-cased text approximating the output of streaming speech recognisers, recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint folds, nested threshold selection and paired cluster bootstrap tests. TurnTurk-GPT outperforms the multilingual detector under both recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation. It outperforms the zero-shot language model only when the test speakers occur in training; on unseen speakers the two are statistically indistinguishable. Removing the suffixes of the turn-final word reduces AP by up to 44%, against 2% for a sentence-internal word, locating the Turkish end-of-turn cue in verb-final morphology. Synthetic dialogue alone yields the weakest trained model, and when a speaker pauses the zero-shot and multilingual baselines remain close to chance. The model and the evaluation protocol are publicly released.

title: Wave Forcing: Towards Speed-of-Light Streaming Video Generation

details.title: Wave Forcing: Towards Speed-of-Light Streaming Video Generation
details.abstract: We introduce Wave Forcing, a training and execution framework for streaming video generation. The key idea is wavefront scheduling: later video chunks begin denoising before earlier chunks finish, using their cleaner intermediate states as causal context. WaveRT sends K/V ahead of use and overlaps communication with computation. After pipeline fill, each concurrent forward round produces one video chunk. Key results: • Quality: On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, 5-step WF maintains overall quality comparable to Rolling Forcing. For 100-second videos, Dynamic Degree improves from 36.63 to 91.45 and Subject Preservation from 92.75 to 97.10. • System efficiency: Our 4-step benchmark on 8×H200 reaches 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS, delivering 7.07× single-GPU E2E throughput.å • Parallelism: Up to 2.53× the throughput of the faster Ulysses/Ring baseline in DiT-only tests with  matched SageAttention+W8A8 backends, step counts and GPU counts. Code, training recipes, and 4-step/5-step checkpoints are available. We welcome feedback and discussion! Project page: https://sjtu-deng-lab.github.io/WaveForcing/ GitHub repo: https://github.com/SJTU-DENG-Lab/WaveForcing

title: Video Generation Meets Agent Harness: Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement

details.title: Video Generation Meets Agent Harness: Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement
details.abstract: Video generation is evolving from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic systems that integrate planning, tool use, and feedback. Meanwhile, video world models are enabling interactive, action-conditioned environments for agents. In this survey, we explore their intersection through the lens of the  agent harness , an executable runtime that manages tools, context, state, feedback, and budgets around video models. We focus on three areas: Agentic Video Generation: Multi-shot planning, production, editing, and evaluation. Agentic World Modeling: Interactive observation, control, and state management. Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI): Improving video outputs, harnesses, models, and the improvement process itself. We also discuss essential agent capabilities and open challenges toward autonomous video production and self-improving video systems. 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40191 🌐 Homepage: https://agentic-videogen.github.io/ 💻 Github: https://github.com/agentic-videogen/awesome-agentic-videogen

Without privileged inputs, out-of-the-box Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves a RoboDojo Score of 31.39, exceeding the published GPT-6 Astra–RoboProbe result of 28.97, while also performing competitively on 19 real-world tasks. Beyond benchmarking, we systematically analyze models across generations, families, and sizes, identifying four general capabilities linked to effective robot use. Our findings suggest that future robot-use agent training should develop these capabilities jointly.

title: Reviso: Not All Visual Evidence Deserves Equal Attention in Video Captioning

details.title: Reviso: Not All Visual Evidence Deserves Equal Attention in Video Captioning
details.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate detailed video captions, yet they may overemphasize minor details while overlooking essential context and key events. We argue that not all visual evidence deserves equal attention, as the importance of visual information depends on the content of each video. Motivated by this observation, we propose Reviso, an agentic video captioning framework that learns what to observe and how to gather relevant visual evidence. From a low-frame- rate global preview, Reviso constructs a hierarchical Context–Focus–Points (CFP) observation plan that identifies the video context, prioritizes key aspects, and defines concrete observation targets and corresponding tools. Guided by this plan, Reviso performs goal-directed active perception by selectively revisiting temporal segments and combining tools for fine-grained inspection. It interprets the acquired evidence, updates its plan as needed, and integrates global and local information to generate the final caption. To learn this observation strategy, we develop a verification-guided pipeline that constructs high-quality training trajectories through factual verification and teacher-guided refinement. We further train Reviso using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), incorporating a key-fact reward for caption quality, a Plan Alignment Reward (PAR) for identifying important observation targets, and an Unproductive Tool-Call Penalty (UTCP) that adjusts observation-cost penalties based on caption quality. Experiments across four video captioning benchmarks show that Reviso outperforms the evaluated open-source baselines, while its generated captions better support downstream video question answering. These findings highlight the effectiveness and potential of priority-guided active observation for video captioning.

title: From Fragmentation to Fusion: A Survey and Roadmap for Omnimodal Embeddings

details.title: From Fragmentation to Fusion: A Survey and Roadmap for Omnimodal Embeddings
details.abstract: Despite shared mathematical foundations, embedding research across text, vision, audio, graphs, tables, and time series remains largely fragmented into modality-specific silos. This survey and position paper argues that embedding research is quietly converging around universal principles: contrastive learning objectives, Transformer backbones, the pretrain–finetune recipe, and an upward shift toward whole semantic units. To evaluate progress toward true unification, we introduce the 3C framework—Coverage, Comparability, and Compositionality—which maps onto three progressive paths: format transformation, cross-modal alignment, and deep joint fusion, our advocated terminus that subsumes alignment and eliminates the modality gap. Reaching this goal will require preserving unique modality-specific structures, cross-pollinating techniques across research communities, and building unified benchmarks that measure true compositional gains.

title: PhotoGuider: Composition-Aware Cropping and 360^{circ} View Framing with Explainable Photographic Assessments

details.title: PhotoGuider: Composition-Aware Cropping and 360^{circ} View Framing with Explainable Photographic Assessments
details.abstract: Traditional image cropping assumes the photograph already contains the composition worth keeping, and asks only where to crop. A full 360° scene offers no such guarantee: the viewing direction in a scene has to be discovered before anything can be framed. We present PhotoGuider, a measure-then-frame method that answers both questions with compact learned scorers over one shared set of composition-aware features. The designed features are extracted using foundation and task-specific vision models and structured into four photographic tokens: Subject, Composition, Aesthetics, and Integrity. Our MLLM explainer is fine-tuned to generate composition-related explanations conditioned on images and measured token assessments. To our knowledge, PhotoGuider is the first method to combine explicit composition-based direction selection in 360∘ panoramas with refined framing, camera-parameter output for native re-rendering, and measurement-conditioned explanations. On two standard 2D cropping benchmarks, PhotoGuider achieves the highest average mIoU performance against ground-truth crops. In a blind ranking study, 120 participants ranked three cropping methods over 100 panoramic scenes from the public Poly Haven HDRI library, placing our framings first in 53.2% of cases, against 27.3% and 19.5% for two strong alternatives. title: CrossSWE: Benchmarking Cross-Repository Joint Development for Coding Agents

details.title: CrossSWE: Benchmarking Cross-Repository Joint Development for Coding Agents
details.abstract: What if we pushed coding agents toward longer-horizon tasks across multiple repositories? 🔗 That's the idea behind CrossSWE ! We extend real-world software engineering tasks beyond a single repository, requiring coding agents to coordinate changes across multiple interconnected repositories. Fixing just one repository isn't enough—agents must make them work together. After all, real-world software development rarely happens in isolation. Why should our benchmarks? 🚀

title: SWE-Trail: History-Guided Trajectory Collection for Coding Agent Training

details.title: SWE-Trail: History-Guided Trajectory Collection for Coding Agent Training
details.abstract: TL;DR: SWE-Trail is a trajectory collector for coding-agent post-training. It uses earlier trajectories to decide where additional collection effort should go, while keeping that history out of the agent's context, so there is no train-test mismatch from training on advice that isn't available at test time. How it works: During a new rollout, history is used to pick a state worth exploring further. The agent proposes candidate next actions from its ordinary context; SWE-Trail briefly executes them from the same checkpoint and decides which route continues. Results: Training a 124B student (initialized from Ling-3.0-flash-base) on SWE-Trail trajectories improves mean resolution by +2.33 pp on SWE-bench Multilingual and +1.60 pp on SWE-bench Pro over independent sampling. Without history, the same pipeline yields more resolved trajectories but only +0.11 pp on Multilingual. The gain comes from using history to guide collection, not from the pipeline alone.

title: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?

details.title: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?
details.abstract: Hi everyone! I'm one of the authors. Our paper asks: when does a video world model's prediction error actually support a claim of physical surprise? The clearest result comes from a controlled support test. A sphere can stop on solid support or fall through a gap; swapping the support reverses which motion is physically possible. Across 256 test configurations , V-JEPA2-G assigns lower mean error to impossible motion on solid support , but higher error to impossible motion over a gap . One development-fixed cutoff reaches 53.9% balanced accuracy on clean clips while falsely flagging about 69% of possible clips . We also examine physical-label readouts, representation geometry, and action/appearance controls. The distinction matters: accessible physical information and action sensitivity do not, by themselves, establish that native prediction error measures physical surprise. These findings concern the tested models and settings—not an absence of physical knowledge. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01815 Project and figures: https://3-ml.github.io/jepa-surprise/ Code and experiment records: https://github.com/3-ml/jepa-surprise I'd be interested in how others validate prediction-error signals before using them for physical-violation detection.

title: Avatar Intelligence: Amplifying Human Agency Through Persistent Personal Agents

details.title: Avatar Intelligence: Amplifying Human Agency Through Persistent Personal Agents
details.abstract: Personal AI agents are increasingly capable of handling long-horizon tasks across applications, yet users often need to invest substantial effort in specifying goals, resolving ambiguity, and verifying outcomes. We argue that progress should be measured by how effectively agents amplify human agency: enabling people to pursue their goals with less routine supervision while retaining control over consequential decisions. We advocate Avatar Intelligence, a paradigm of persistent personal agents that represent users’ goals, values, and constraints through sustained decision delegation across contexts and time. We describe a maturity roadmap fromhuman-directedexecutiontoautonomousoperationwithindelegateddomains, andintroduce the Agentic Oversight Index (AOI) as a framework for evaluating delivered value against agent- side operational cost and human oversight burden. We identify three core research challenges: identity-continuous personalization that carries user preferences across tasks, user-situated evolution through Rehearsal Engineering, and safety mechanisms that combine technical control with accountability and recourse. These directions define a research agenda for reliable decision delegation to personal agents across tasks and over time.

title: FLAMIA: FLAsh MIcroscaling Attention for Fast and Causally Safe Training on Blackwell

details.title: FLAMIA: FLAsh MIcroscaling Attention for Fast and Causally Safe Training on Blackwell
details.abstract: FLAMIA (FLAsh MIcroscaling Attention) adapts FlashAttention to Blackwell’s FP8/FP4 hardware. Its main design choices are: Selective low precision. Two main training paths: MXFP8, or NVFP4 for query–key score computation and its backward recomputation, with FP8 for the remaining products. All-FP4 adds quantization overhead and slightly worsens loss. Reusable quantized representations. Power-of-two scales shared over blocks of 32 tokens across all head channels—and 32 × 32 blocks for score gradients—allow FP8 operands to serve both matrix orientations, reducing duplicate quantization and memory traffic. Quantization-aware causality. Shared scales can leak future-token information despite causal masking. Local scales, saturation avoidance, and per-key scale folding mitigate leakage; exact causal options remove residual dependencies in supported batched calls. Consistent forward and backward numerics. Probability recomputation follows matching quantization, tiling, scaling, and exponential conventions. High single-step gradient similarity alone does not guarantee stable training. Hardware-aware kernels. Fused quantization, overlap between softmax and matrix multiplication, and a low-precision backward pass using two cooperative thread arrays reduce overhead and improve GPU utilization. Direct packed-document support. Document-local quantization avoids repacking, while GPU scheduling balances work across variable document lengths. FLAMIA achieves approximately 1.06–1.42× faster combined forward/backward attention , including quantization, across the evaluated causal packed-document workloads.

title: DecisionRank: On-Policy Distillation for Decision-Model Rerankers

details.title: DecisionRank: On-Policy Distillation for Decision-Model Rerankers
details.abstract: Decision models target structured tasks by directly predicting choices or scores, avoiding autoregressive decoding latency. However, transferring a generative LLM's ranking knowledge to a decision model remains challenging: the teacher expresses preferences through a ranked list of document ID sequences, while the student determines the ranking using scores from the first-token position. To bridge this gap, we introduce DecisionRank, a decision model trained through item-space on-policy distillation (OPD). Item-space OPD constructs the student's rollout by sorting its document scores into a ranked sequence. A generative teacher takes the resulting ranking list as inputs and provides conditional feedback to directly supervise those scores. Combined with offline ranking supervision, DecisionRank achieves state-of-the-art performance on both general and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks such as TREC DL, BEIR, and BRIGHT. Across four benchmarks, item-space OPD consistently outperforms alternative training objectives. Even at 1.7B parameters, DecisionRank surpasses its 27B generative teacher on TREC DL19-23. At 8B, it outperforms its generative listwise counterpart while running 24.5× faster on TREC DL and 16.7× faster on BRIGHT.

title: DeFT-RAG: Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers

details.title: DeFT-RAG: Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers
details.abstract: DeFT-RAG asks a different question about multi-hop RAG: instead of planning all sub-questions and their dependencies in advance, what if the LLM writes just one self-contained sub-question at a time? Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, so it never has to be rewritten, and its answer stays correct for any question that asks it. The rest of the work moves outside the LLM: a QA table updated by rules keeps track of what is known, and a fine-tuned 4B decision model makes the yes/no decisions and estimates question depth. A QA cache reuses answers across questions. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among 13 baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6, including +5.2 points on MuSiQue over Hi-Q, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a shared QA cache, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, reducing LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy. 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37826 💻 Code: https://github.com/Dingyi-Kang/DeFT-RAG 🤗 Decision model: https://huggingface.co/Dingy-Kang/DeFT-RAG-DM-4B

title: BYOD: Build Your Own DLM - Efficient Autoregressive-to-Diffusion Language Model Conversion

details.title: BYOD: Build Your Own DLM - Efficient Autoregressive-to-Diffusion Language Model Conversion
details.abstract: BYOD: Build your own diffusion language model in Google Colab Can an existing instruction model learn to generate text through diffusion in a few hours on one GPU? In BYOD: Build Your Own DLM , we convert Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Ministral 8B into bidirectional masked-diffusion language models. Every pretrained weight stays frozen: training updates only LoRA adapters, representing 4.1–5.8% of the final model parameters . The four primary conversions each took 3.1–4.0 hours on one GPU in Google Colab . We want other people to be able to train, inspect, and experiment with these models too. The training notebook and interactive demos are available now. Try the fine-tuned diffusion models before training your own: These demos run directly in your browser: Model Interactive demo Gemma 2 9B Try BYOD-Gemma Llama 3.1 8B Try BYOD-Llama Qwen2.5 7B Try BYOD-Qwen Ministral 8B Try BYOD-Ministral Instead of appending one token at a time, the model starts with a masked answer and fills positions through successive denoising steps, with a flexible inference budget. Try the same prompt with different step budgets and see how it influences inference speed and quality. The hosted demos also include experimental decoding options beyond the paper’s evaluation settings. For related demos, try our earlier LAD model , which also enabled the changing of unmasked tokens. Train your own model Open the training notebook in Google Colab · Code and instructions The notebook has been designed to make it as easy as possible to help you train your own DLM. No coding is needed, you only need to run each code cell: Choose a model. Use the provided tokenized training data, or configure your own instruction–response dataset. Train while watching the loss curve to see if the model keeps improving. Open the interactive inference interface via the notebook step 6 and try out your model. You can also stop a run early and still use it in the interface. Quick mode trains smaller Llama, Gemma, or Qwen models and rank-128 LoRA for initial experiments. Paper mode uses the original 7B–9B models and rank-1024 adapters and needs a paid GPU; our paper runs used a 96 GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 . What did we find? The same conversion recipe works across all four families. All four generate from fully masked answers and use information to the right of a masked position in our controlled attention test. BYOD-Gemma comes within 1.3 percentage points of LLaDA on our nine-task average: 50.6% versus 51.9%, evaluated in the same harness. The unchanged AR parents still perform better on average, with particularly large conversion gaps in mathematics and code. Figure 1: Task-level accuracy in the matched evaluation. Performance depends on both the task and the converted model family. Generation at a low number of inference steps: At 64 denoising steps for 128 output tokens, externally scored perplexity is 8.3–11.1 for BYOD, versus 4.1 for LLaDA and 2.2–3.0 for the AR parents. Increasing the denoising budget improves the results, but our low-cost conversion still leaves a quality gap. Figure 3: Generation quality across inference budgets. Lower perplexity and higher Distinct-1 are better; crosses mark the AR parents. We hope BYOD makes diffusion-model experiments easier to start: change a backbone, try different training data, inspect a denoising trajectory, and see what improves. Start with the Colab notebook · Read the paper · Get the code

WorldFlow is dedicated to scaling the generalization of explicit 3D object kinematics. By bridging pixel-level evolution and a shared 3D motion space, it delivers highly robust, platform-independent 3D trajectory forecasting.

title: MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads

details.title: MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads
details.abstract: Multi-agent collaboration fundamentally reshapes LLM serving workloads through dynamic dependencies, synchronization, and context sharing—beyond what conventional request-level benchmarks can capture. We introduce MAServeBench , a benchmark featuring composable hierarchical collaboration patterns and dependency-preserving Semantic Traces for reproducible serving evaluation and architecture simulation. Our GPU/NPU studies reveal how collaboration affects compute efficiency, KV cache pressure, and end-to-end task performance. We hope this work helps guide the design of next-generation serving systems and hardware for agentic AI. Feedback and discussions are very welcome!

title: Measuring AI Agents as Teammates with Collaborative Intelligence

details.title: Measuring AI Agents as Teammates with Collaborative Intelligence
details.abstract: Most benchmarks measure what a model can do on its own. We built the Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark to measure how well an AI agent works as a teammate . It has 240 tasks across 8 dimensions of teamwork, from refusing an unsafe shortcut to checking the work a weaker model left behind. Each task comes from a real record or an existing benchmark (aviation accident reports, clinical cases, coding tasks, negotiations) and has a verifiable outcome. Models are scored only on tasks they can solve alone with full information, so the score isolates teamwork from individual capability. What we found across 18 closed- and open-weight models Every model has clear weaknesses as a teammate. The best, Gemini 4 Argon at high effort, scores 82.2 out of 100. Frontier models almost always refuse unsafe shortcuts and report misconduct, yet they reach the best overall deal in only 14% of conflicts. Their pass rate drops from 97% to 81% when they take over a task in which a weaker model has cheated. Models with nearly the same general capability differ by up to 11 points as teammates.

title: TinyAstral: Transferring Self-Evolving Harnesses to Tiny Generalist Manipulation Agents

The 4B student stays close to its teacher on six manipulation benchmarks at about one fifth of the compute, and runs closed loop on a real arm. Code, weights and data are released.

title: Lab2Sim: Turning Real-World Experiment Videos into Interactive Virtual Experiments

details.title: Lab2Sim: Turning Real-World Experiment Videos into Interactive Virtual Experiments
details.abstract: Science experiment videos demonstrate how experiments are performed, but offer no direct interaction for learners. Turning them into virtual experiments requires not only reproducing the observed apparatus and state changes, but also enforcing the preconditions governing each operation. We introduce Lab2Sim, a benchmark of 218 science experiment videos with evidence-grounded specifications and 11,881 rubric items. To address this task, we propose EduVideo2Code, which extracts experimental procedures hierarchically, encodes them as explicit state machines to guide code generation, and refines the resulting pages through execution-based verification. Experiments show that existing multimodal models readily generate runnable pages but struggle to faithfully reconstruct experimental apparatus. EduVideo2Code consistently improves all four evaluation dimensions across two backbone models, with apparatus fidelity gains of 24.15 points.

title: Library of Layers (LoL): Adaptively Ordering Transformer Layers at Runtime

details.title: Library of Layers (LoL): Adaptively Ordering Transformer Layers at Runtime
details.abstract: Computer programmers chain together the same reusable computational primitives, for example, conditional statements or loops, but in different orders to implement different algorithms. In contrast, existing language model architectures always execute their layers in the same order. We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), an architecture that dynamically orders its layers during inference to solve the problem at hand. LoL has a single hyperparameter, the size of its global library of transformer blocks, that allows it to transition seamlessly between parameter reuse and sparsity, generalizing the parameter-efficiency and FLOPs-efficiency tradeoffs of dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture of experts architectures in one unified family. We show that LoL achieves competitive performance with all three above baselines when pretrained on text data. On synthetic sudoku and maze data, we observe that the model employs distinct layer orderings to implement different solution strategies, and we can intervene on routing to force a model to apply a specific solution strategy to a problem instance. In a multilingual natural language setting, we find that LoL chooses different layer order patterns based on language and script. Similarly, we train LoL on safety data and fit probes to its router outputs, finding that these probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC. LoL provides a path toward a future in which models dynamically compose their own computational graph, enabling more efficient and controllable reasoning.

title: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Teacher Evolution

details.title: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Teacher Evolution
details.abstract: We wanted to solve a frustrating problem in On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD): the "self-teacher" model often gets blinded by the privileged context and gives pretty unreliable, overconfident token-level guidance, which ends up misleading the student model. To fix this, we proposed TESD (Teacher-Evolution Self-Distillation): We let the teacher evolve dynamically by optimizing it with environment feedback. We automatically down-weight those training samples where the teacher's guidance is deemed unreliable. As a result, TESD consistently beats standard token-level distillation (like SDPO) and even sequence-level RL (like GRPO) across benchmarks like SciKnowEval and Tooluse.

title: Where Do Vision Language Models Fail at 3D Reasoning?

details.title: Where Do Vision Language Models Fail at 3D Reasoning?
details.abstract: Where Do Vision Language Models Fail at 3D Reasoning? Vision-language models can get individual judgments right while struggling to recover and consistently use the exact properties of a 3D object. To characterize this gap, we introduce BedBench, a controlled benchmark of thirteen procedurally generated tasks spanning individual judgments and composite answers. Across twelve open-weight and four frontier models, per-color counting exposes a pronounced weakness: humans achieve 93.3% accuracy, compared with 7.2% for the best model. Targeted fine-tuning raises one model's accuracy from 3.0% to 68.6%, but reveals a further difficulty: its answers about the most common colors remain inconsistent with its own per-color counts. Supplying those counts as text improves its judgments, showing that recovering a property does not mean using it consistently. Reasoning, scaling, and added visual cues each improve individual judgments, but none makes exact answers reliable. To locate the difficulty, we probe Qwen3.5-27B: exact per-color counts remain recoverable at the language model's input, yet the model's answers rarely recover them (65.0% for the probe vs. 3.0% for the model). Image-removal controls further show that some apparent successes require no visual evidence. These findings motivate evaluating 3D reasoning by exact correctness, consistent use, and image dependence, rather than accuracy alone

title: LEANGUARD: Lean-Verified Guardrails for Tool-Using Agents

details.title: LEANGUARD: Lean-Verified Guardrails for Tool-Using Agents
details.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents often execute actions that their domain policies forbid. We present LeanGuard, a runtime that checks every proposed tool call against a policy written in Lean4 before the call reaches the environment. Policies combine state predicates with scoped past-time temporal operators over the execution history, evaluation is fail-closed, and the decision procedure is proved equivalent to a LeanLTL semantics. A denied call can be corrected in two ways. With feedback, the agent receives the violated rule and a hint; with proof-guided repair, Lean metaprogramming searches for a nearby call that preserves the user's intent and proves that the policy admits it, without the model. On Tau-Bench with five Qwen models (0.8B-27B), unguarded agents execute at least 33 calls that the Lean policy forbids, while LeanGuard executes none; with feedback, task success does not change significantly. On DTap, LeanGuard reduces direct prompt-injection success from 57.9% to 5.9%, and in telecom, where benign tasks need no writes, benign success is unchanged. Feedback reduces repeated blocked calls and raises task success for four of five models over a bare denial. On replayed denials, repair proves an admissible edit for 88 of 252 denials caused by argument values, in a median of 2ms.

title: TaoMate-FVSR:Audio-Guided Facial Video Restoration

details.title: TaoMate-FVSR:Audio-Guided Facial Video Restoration
details.abstract: Low-quality facial videos suffer from missing fine details, while AI-generated videos may additionally contain implausible teeth and lip movements that do not match the speech. Restoring the mouth region is particularly challenging: enhancing existing details can preserve structural errors, whereas regenerating them risks changing facial identity and articulation. We propose an audio-guided facial video restoration framework that reconstructs unreliable mouth details and aligns lip movements with the speech while preserving facial identity and temporal consistency. Built on a video diffusion transformer, our framework mixes input video latents with noise to retain useful source information while allowing corrupted details to be regenerated. Audio guides lip movements, reference images constrain facial appearance, and previously generated frames promote temporal consistency. We train the model in two stages, first learning visual restoration from degraded images and videos, then learning audio-guided lip correction from degraded dubbed videos. The resulting model supports both restoration with the original audio and visual dubbing with replacement audio. On talking-head restoration benchmarks, our method achieves the lowest LPIPS and DISTS and the best lip synchronization scores among the evaluated restoration baselines. Qualitative results on AI-generated videos further show improvements in facial detail and mouth-region appearance, including clearer tooth boundaries and lip contours.

title: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos?

details.title: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos?
details.abstract: Can LLM agents learn from tutorial videos, just like humans do? 🎥🧠 We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a non-parametric continual learning framework that enables frozen LLM agents to learn from instructional videos without updating model parameters. TAL transforms instructional videos into structured, persistent tutorialbook memories through adversarial knowledge-gap probing and targeted memory refinement, where challenging questions expose gaps in the tutorialbook memory and drive iterative improvement. By turning tutorial videos into reusable knowledge, TAL takes a step toward AI agents that can continuously learn and improve from human teaching throughout their lifetime.
