title: When Morphs Look Better: Face Image Quality as a Training-Free Signal for Morphing Attack Detection

details.title: When Morphs Look Better: Face Image Quality as a Training-Free Signal for Morphing Attack Detection
details.abstract: Face image quality assessment (FIQA) estimates the utility of a face image for face recognition and is trained without morphs. We evaluate 17 FIQA methods from all current FIQA categories as training-free single-image morphing attack detection (MAD) scores on 20 morphing attack sets from two datasets, FRLL and FEI, including five diffusion-based attack sets. Each quality score is used directly as the MAD decision score. Only a threshold is set, on bona fide images. The score direction of each method is fixed in advance from its definition and never chosen per attack, so that cases in which morphs receive higher quality than bona fide images remain visible. A signed separation reports both the strength and the direction of the score shift caused by morphing.

title: RoboColosseum: Evaluating Physical Intelligence at Scale In-The-Wild

details.title: RoboColosseum: Evaluating Physical Intelligence at Scale In-The-Wild
details.abstract: General-purpose robot policies must work across robots, tasks, and environments, yet the variation that makes physical trials informative also makes them difficult to reproduce. We introduce RoboColosseum, a distributed evaluation framework that combines unified policy serving and standardized protocols across a network of locally operated robots in diverse environments. Our initial study evaluates five vision-language-action (VLA) policies and three frontier AI agents across four embodiments (SO-101, Franka, Bimanual-YAM, and G1 Humanoid). The Open Track compares models without task-specific adaptation in blinded, pairwise trials under matched local conditions. The Fine-tune Track measures how well VLA policies adapt to 20 tasks when each policy receives the same 100 demonstrations per task. Across 5,699 Open Track comparisons at 124 sites, frontier agents rival specialized VLA policies, though all systems struggle to complete open-world tasks reliably. After fine-tuning, GR00T N1.7 leads on SO-101 and π0.5 leads on Franka and Bimanual-YAM. Policy rankings show weak agreement across embodiment-specific task suites (Kendall’s W = 0.24). Open Track rankings poorly predict relative performance after fine-tuning, with substantial rank reversals on all three embodiments shared between tracks. Measuring partial progress reveals differences that task success alone misses. On the G1 Humanoid, no policy completes any of the five tasks, yet average progress ranges from 13.3% to 23.2% across policies. Open Track rankings stabilize as trials accumulate, and active matchmaking achieves comparable ranking agreement with substantially fewer physical trials than uniform sampling. These results show how distributed physical evaluation can reveal where robot policies generalize, how well they adapt to new tasks, and how far they progress on tasks they fail to complete.

title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents

details.title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents
details.abstract: Happy to share our latest work on agent environment synthesis: 🌟 ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents Most existing environment synthesis methods are data-centric: they first build the underlying database, then synthesize tools and tasks. Tool interfaces easily drift from reality, and it is hard to form tasks that span environments. ToolSpace takes the opposite approach. It first collects tools from real call traces, then chains real tool sets into a tool universe, and finally synthesizes the underlying database on demand. This preserves authenticity while flexibly generating verifiable tasks across any environment × any tool. 💡 Key methods 1️⃣ Tool universe exploration: mine tool dependencies from real traces and link them into a tool-world graph; synthesize databases only for environments that change state. 2️⃣ Verifiable task synthesis: walk the graph with state-aware traversal and backtracking, decompile executable tool chains into tasks and verification scripts, and keep environment state continuous. The same chain can yield high-quality SFT data and mixed-environment RL data. 3️⃣ Harder evaluation benchmarks: ToolSpace seamlessly upgrades two frontier benchmarks into AutomationBench Pro and τ³-Bench Banking Pro. Strong existing models all score below 40, setting a harder bar for the field. 📊 Experiments ✅ We evaluate ToolSpace-8B, 35B, and 744B on 7 long-horizon tool benchmarks. ToolSpace-744B averages 56.6, on par with Claude Opus 5. ✅ ToolSpace-744B: AutomationBench 54.7, Harvey LAB 27.5, SkillsBench 67.8, OfficeQA Pro 67.1, JobBench 57.5. ✅ Agent performance scales as environment and data scale grow. We welcome discussion and feedback. Code and models are open-sourced 👏👏👏 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.05036 🌐 Project page: https://toolspace-agent.github.io/ 💻 GitHub: https://github.com/dongguanting/ToolSpace 🤗 Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/collections/dongguanting/toolspace

title: EvoTeam: Multi-Agent Collaboration via Evolving Teams

details.title: EvoTeam: Multi-Agent Collaboration via Evolving Teams
details.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on collaboration among specialized agents to solve complex tasks. Existing methods improve MAS by refining the prompts, skills, and execution strategies of individual agents based on task feedback. However, improving individual agents does not necessarily lead to better team collaboration. Recent studies have therefore extended evolution to the collaboration level, using collective execution experience to adjust team organization, and inter-agent interactions. Nevertheless, evolving collaboration across heterogeneous tasks remains challenging, as existing approaches often constrain team reorganization within a shared structure and reuse interaction rules across incompatible team contexts. In this paper, we propose EvoTeam, a collaboration-centric evolution framework that jointly evolves team organization, interaction rules, and individual agent skills through execution experience. It maintains a library of reusable teams, selecting or creating agent teams and guiding collaboration through team-specific interaction rules. Collaboration experience accumulates within compatible team contexts, while individual skills remain reusable across teams. Experiments across four benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness. Our code is available at https://github.com/DEEP-JLU/EvoTeam .

title: VidUEU-Agent: A Data-Curation Agent for Multimodal Understanding, Editing, and Unified Tasks

details.title: VidUEU-Agent: A Data-Curation Agent for Multimodal Understanding, Editing, and Unified Tasks
details.abstract: 🚀 We are excited to share our latest work: “VidUEU-Agent: A Data-Curation Agent for Multimodal Understanding, Editing, and Unified Tasks”! The scarcity and high annotation cost of high-quality multimodal instruction data remain major bottlenecks for multimodal model development. Raw videos contain rich visual knowledge and temporal information, but transforming them into accurate, verifiable, and task-oriented instruction data remains challenging. To address this, we introduce VidUEU-Agent, an agentic data-curation framework that automatically constructs instruction data from raw videos for multimodal understanding, image editing, and unified understanding-and-generation tasks. 🔑 Key Highlights 🎬 Four-Stage Data Construction Pipeline: VidUEU-Agent performs global perception to analyze video structure and filter low-quality shots, mines informative keyframes and multimodal signals, constructs structured metadata, and routes each metadata entry to suitable task types for instruction synthesis. Agent planning, tool use, and multi-stage quality control support the entire process. 🔍 Evidence-Grounded Data Synthesis: The framework combines vision-language models with visual tools for quality assessment, semantic analysis, and information verification. During instruction synthesis, the model cites the evidence signals it uses, improving data traceability and factual consistency. 🔄 Autonomous Iteration with Training Feedback: VidUEU-Agent uses downstream training and evaluation results to identify weaknesses and refine data distributions across capabilities, domains, and task types. Across four iterations, each using 30K samples to fine-tune BAGEL from the same initial checkpoint, performance improves overall on the three feedback benchmarks: 📦 VidUEU-100K Dataset: Using this pipeline, we construct VidUEU-100K from 8,268 diverse videos, containing nearly 20,000 dense metadata annotations and 100,000 instruction samples: 40K understanding, 30K editing, and 30K unified samples, spanning nine task paradigms and five scenario categories. Our work demonstrates how raw videos can be transformed into diverse, evidence-grounded instruction data through agent planning, tool augmentation, and training-feedback-driven refinement. We hope VidUEU-Agent and VidUEU-100K provide a scalable and reproducible foundation for developing unified multimodal models. 📄 Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04418 💻 Code: https://github.com/LRuca/VidUEU-Agent 🤗 Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Lruca/VidUEU100k We welcome feedback and discussions!

details.title: WebHarbor: Docking Real Websites for Evolving GUI Agent Environments
details.abstract: We introduce WebHarbor, a suite of 153 executable, dockerized website environments that reconstruct the visual interfaces, content, and workflows of real-world web services, plus 3,518 tasks for evaluating and training GUI web agents. Why: live-web evaluation is unstable. In our runs, about 38% of Online-Mind2Web tasks were blocked by bot detection, and 22% of WebVoyager tasks were outdated. Core contributions: Environments: task-driven human-agent collaboration. Coding agents implement each site, and human reviewers audit visual fidelity, functional correctness, and task validity. 57 contributors from 26 affiliations built the suite in five months. Each environment averages 37.3 pages and 1,319.9 images, the most of any compared suite. Tasks: multi-step and post-authentication workflows (accounts, bookings, transactions) that live-web benchmarks largely lack, graded by verifiers that check the final answer and the state changes, with fast resets for RL. Results: trained with RL only in WebHarbor, WebHarbor-4B reaches a 75.8 average on WebVoyager and Online-Mind2Web, 5.2 points above the live-web-trained OpenWebRL-4B and 22.2 above the shared SFT checkpoint. title: "Shall We Approve?" Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents

details.title: "Shall We Approve?" Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents
details.abstract: Does a coding agent really know what its next command will do? Approving every command by hand does not scale: Claude Code users approve 93% of permission prompts anyway. So agents now rely on automated approvers, such as Claude Code's Auto Mode, rule-based checkers, and guardrail models. All of them judge the text of the command. Yet a command's behavior is decided by the scripts it invokes and the workspace it runs in, and the same command can be harmless in one project and destructive in another. We propose Caper , which approves a command after seeing what it does. Each command is pre-executed in a snapshotted sandbox under system-call tracing. An LLM approver reviews a compact report of the observed effects: file changes, network attempts, and reads of secrets. Allowed commands are committed; blocked ones are rolled back, and the agent gets a reason it can act on. Compared with six existing systems, Caper has the lowest harmful-outcome rate on SABER (6.7% vs. at least 14.8%) and on YoloFS-Ext, our benchmark that hides harm inside the tools agents are asked to run (7.8% vs. at least 35.3%). It blocks only 1.0% of the safe twins. Code and data: https://github.com/wudaoz/Caper

details.title: PrimeSim: A Generalist World Model Simulator from Large-Scale Cross-Embodiment Demonstrations
details.abstract: PrimeSim is an action-conditioned, multiview world model that runs as a robot simulator. It starts from a pretrained video generator, midtrains on 30,110 hours across 22 platforms, then posttrains into a causal few-step generator. Posttraining combines self-rollout training, so the model learns from its own generated histories rather than only real frames, with a selected KV-cache memory that carries context across chunks. Inference runs at over 10 FPS with all three camera views. PrimeSim scores first overall on EWMBench and leads four of five WorldSimProbe suites against state-of-the-art baselines. Rollouts stay coherent over long horizons and transfer to held-out platforms within 100-200 gradient steps. We also use the model as an environment for reinforcement learning: GRPO post-training inside PrimeSim raises LIBERO success from 61.7% to 73.2%, and the model's success predictions track the physics simulator closely enough to rank policies. All experiments are in simulation (AgiBot G2, LIBERO, RoboTwin); no physical robot is used, and closed-loop hardware deployment is future work. title: Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems

details.title: Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems
details.abstract: When a foundation model moves into a new domain, there's usually little expert-written data or reliable supervision to train on. Recursa adapts to the domain by learning from its own experience, without human experts or a stronger teacher model. A knowledge repository stores what the system learns: domain-specific skills, instructions on when to use them, memories of past tasks, and reflections on what to improve. Bootstrapping: the system builds the repository from domain materials and practices on tasks it generates from them. This targets the knowledge gap. Recursive self-improvement: parallel learners run tasks and propose local improvements, which are validated and merged back into the repository. This targets the behavior gap. The system's own model drives the whole process, including improving how it learns. On Harvey LAB's Firm Knowledge benchmark, Recursa raises the all-pass rate on held-out test tasks from 30.0% to 55.0% with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and from 35.0% to 46.0% with Qwen3.8-Flash. title: Every Token Needs Its Own Teacher: Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-distillation

details.title: Every Token Needs Its Own Teacher: Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-distillation
details.abstract: On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) has proven effective for post-training large language models by constructing a teacher conditioned on privileged references. However, existing approaches keep the teacher fixed either throughout training by consistently exposing it to the full reference, or within each response by adaptively varying partial reference exposure only across responses. In this paper, we argue that neither of them is sufficient. Instead, every token needs its own teacher, as the teacher preference can vary token by token within the same response. Through a teacher-intervention pilot study, we validate that the teacher preference differs across tokens, and reveal that a preferred teacher can be identified for each token through majority voting and KL-based selection. Motivated by these findings, we propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. Our method constructs a multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers, and enables every token to adaptively select its preferred teacher during training. Experiments with Qwen3 models on mathematical reasoning tasks show that MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches with an average gain of up to +5.9 over the base model, highlighting the importance of adapting teacher supervision at the token level. The code is available at https://github.com/xingzhejun/MTA-OPSD .

We introduce PaperTrajectory-2026, covering 6,959 paper trajectories across five AI conferences, with automatic annotations along 14 revision dimensions. Evaluating eight AI reviewers, we find that most revisions annotated as major improvements receive unchanged scores, with weak agreement across reviewers on the direction of score changes. Even when revisions earn higher scores, a brief negative user opinion can erase or reverse that advantage. Our study highlights the need for AI reviewers whose judgments track substantive improvements and remain stable when the scientific evidence is unchanged.

title: Is Your Long-Horizon Benchmark Really Deep? Measuring and Synthesizing Depth in Terminal Tasks

details.title: Is Your Long-Horizon Benchmark Really Deep? Measuring and Synthesizing Depth in Terminal Tasks
details.abstract: Long-horizon terminal tasks are used to evaluate and train agents. Human-curated datasets are scarce, so many synthesis methods have emerged. They usually measure the length of a task by the turns a model needs to pass it, and its difficulty by labels the LLM sets during generation. We find, however, that the turn count largely reflects the habits of the model, not only the demands of the task, and that the labels barely track how often models pass. We describe a terminal task by its work, the number of operations it requires, and its depth, the number of turns that must happen in sequence because the commands of each turn can only be chosen after reading the output of the previous one. Estimating depth as the smallest turn cap, stated to the agent, under which the task passes, we audit 734 tasks from six existing datasets. Synthesis has mostly added work, not depth: 94% of the solved synthetic tasks pass within three turns, yet depth, unlike the turn count, predicts difficulty beyond work. We propose DEPTH, in which a generation agent writes each task one segment at a time in a real software environment, carrying out each segment before writing it and starting the next from the state it leaves. Our 105 tasks exceed every audited dataset in depth and work, and none of six current models passes half of them. Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on runs from these tasks improves it on two terminal benchmarks.

It introduces the tilted novice, a low-rank input-dependent replacement for pruned experts, which improves over MoNE’s constant replacement with only ~1.2–1.8% additional parameters, while showing that no single replacement operator universally dominates.

title: Is Forgetting Unified? Exploring Concept Unlearning in Unified Multimodal Models

details.title: Is Forgetting Unified? Exploring Concept Unlearning in Unified Multimodal Models
details.abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks require agents to learn, reason, and generalize robustly across complex real-world environments. However, existing approaches often struggle with partial observability, fragmented spatial reasoning, and inefficient integration of heterogeneous memories, limiting their capacity for long-horizon adaptation. To address this, we introduce RoboMemory, a brain-inspired framework that unifies Temporal, Spatial, Semantic, and Episodic memory for efficient long-horizon planning and interactive learning. Its core innovations are a comprehensive memory system designed for embodied tasks, and a dynamic spatial knowledge graph for scalable, consistent memory updates. Extensive experiments on EmbodiedBench show that RoboMemory improves the average success rate of Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Ins by 26.5 percentage points and achieves performance comparable to strong closed-source VLM agents. Real-world trials further suggest RoboMemory's potential for interactive environmental learning by reusing accumulated experience across repeated task attempts. These results demonstrate RoboMemory as a scalable memory-augmented framework for embodied agents, improving long-horizon planning and cumulative learning in complex interactive environments.

title: Where to Learn and How Far to Roll Out: Efficient Adaptive Training for GUI Agents

details.title: Where to Learn and How Far to Roll Out: Efficient Adaptive Training for GUI Agents
details.abstract: Trajectory-level GRPO is a common approach for training multi-step GUI agents, but repeatedly rolling out complete trajectories from the task root can be inefficient: task-level rewards provide coarse supervision over which intermediate decisions require improvement, while already-mastered prefixes are repeatedly re-executed before reaching difficult states. We introduce a two-stage adaptive training framework that jointly addresses where to learn and how far to roll out. We first construct reusable intermediate checkpoints from successful expert trajectories and select informative pivots using action disagreement, which measures uncertainty directly from sampled GUI actions. Stage I performs one-step RL at these pivots to improve uncertain local decisions. Stage II then progressively expands policy responsibility through adaptive Local, Suffix, and Root training according to task progress. Recoverable checkpoints enable repeated training from intermediate states without replaying the preceding trajectory. Across MobileGym and CUA-Gym-Hub, our method reduces environment interaction by 56-61% relative to Vanilla GRPO while improving task performance, demonstrating that jointly allocating training across states and rollout ranges can substantially improve GUI-agent RL efficiency.

title: SeMo3D: Unifying 3D Generation, Editing, and Completion via Selective Modeling

details.title: SeMo3D: Unifying 3D Generation, Editing, and Completion via Selective Modeling
details.abstract: 3D generation, editing, and completion are typically treated as regenerating the complete 3D asset under task-specific constraints, even when only a local region needs modification. This leads to task isolation, inconsistency in content that should remain unchanged, and dependence on task-specific paired data. We address these issues with a key observation: the three tasks all synthesize a designated region while keeping the rest intact---the full region for generation, the target region for editing, and the missing region for completion. We term this paradigm Selective Modeling and build SeMo3D upon it; it naturally unifies the three tasks, preserves unchanged content by construction, and enables training without paired editing or completion data, since any 3D asset can be partitioned into a selected region and its context. For training, we propose region-selective denoising, which randomly selects regions of varying sizes on standard 3D assets and applies noise and loss only to them, jointly learning all three tasks. For architecture, we propose Omni3DiT, a multi-condition 3D diffusion transformer that distinguishes regions to create from those to retain and fuses image, text, and point guidance for fine-grained control. Experiments across three benchmarks show SeMo3D surpasses state-of-the-art methods on all tasks, delivering multimodal controllability in generation and strong consistency and accuracy in editing and completion. SeMo3D further serves as a unified modeling tool for agents, enabling efficient 3D creation through natural-language interaction. We introduce an agent that treats AlphaFold 3 as a black-box experimental instrument, autonomously analyzing and reorganizing MSAs through biological reasoning and iterative, confidence-guided experimentation. Evaluated on 1,015 protein–protein interfaces across three benchmarks, our approach consistently improves prediction accuracy over standard AF3 pipelines while using 60% fewer MSA sequences on average . title: From Pixels to Actions - Towards Native Vision-Language-Action Policies

details.title: From Pixels to Actions - Towards Native Vision-Language-Action Policies
details.abstract: NEO-VLA challenges a common assumption in VLA design: that action should rely on visual representations distilled for semantic understanding. Our findings suggest that effective control instead benefits from early visual computation. Native representations transfer well to action even when frozen, while exposing intermediate features in encoder-based VLMs does not yield comparable gains. This highlights the importance of how visual representations are formed, rather than encoder removal alone. Moreover, NEO-VLA shows strong robustness to visual shifts but remains challenged by changes in spatial configurations and task goals. Together, these findings suggest that the next frontier of embodied intelligence lies in bridging perception and flexible control, motivating native representations that are intrinsically action-relevant.

title: Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit

details.title: Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit
details.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.

title: What Does Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improve in LLM Agents?

details.title: What Does Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improve in LLM Agents?
details.abstract: While multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning (RL) excels on long-horizon tasks, its performance gains remain highly sensitive to interaction constraints. Evaluating across sampling breadth K and interaction depth T via Pass@(K,T), we show that trajectory-level RL advantages depend on sufficient turn budgets, diminishing significantly when budgets tighten. Besides, agentic RL does not uniformly elevate single-step decision quality; rather, its strength concentrates in error recovery and long-horizon resilience. To mitigate the deployment risks caused by this budget dependence, we provide a preliminary discussion on the benefits and limitations of process supervision signals and introduce BudgetMix RL as an alternative that varies interaction budgets during training. Experiments demonstrate that BudgetMix RL achieves robust performance across diverse execution settings.

title: PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data

details.title: PyRUA-DataFarm: LLM Agent as a Cost-Efficient Teleoperator for Real-Ready Robot Data
details.abstract: Teleoperation remains the default way to collect robot demonstrations, but every episode costs robot and operator time, and every new task starts from scratch. We ask whether a coding agent can take over the teleoperator's job. In our DataFarm, the agent receives a data request and one calibration episode of the robot in the target scene and rebuilds the task in simulation: it writes the scene, an expert controller, and a success judge. The simulator supplies exact actions, and a video model conditioned on real images renders each rollout as photographic video, generating all camera views together consistently. The output is real-ready data: synchronized camera views labelled with the robot's actions, on which a policy can be trained directly and deployed on the real robot. Independent judges certify the expert and every rendered episode before admission. On five real-robot tasks, policies trained only on farm data match policies trained on as many teleoperated episodes (93 vs. 84 successes in 100 trials), and under an unseen tablecloth and coloured light they keep 87 successes where the teleoperation-trained policies fall to 46. Adapting a task is fully automatic and costs $21 of API usage on average, paid once per task, plus $5 for a render contract; every further episode costs $0.80 on average for simulation, rendering, and review, with no robot or operator. One hour of three-view data for a task costs $107 on average, these costs included, slightly below a quote of $117 for teleoperation in China and below $290 in labour alone in North America.

title: EmoReward: Self-Evolving Reward Calibration for Emotional Video Generation RL

details.title: EmoReward: Self-Evolving Reward Calibration for Emotional Video Generation RL
details.abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has advanced generative model post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, but evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Existing approaches typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that poorly capture emotional intent and can invite reward hacking, while RLHF is difficult to scale and subject to individual aesthetic differences that complicate the calibration of facial, body motion, and chromatic cues across narrative contexts. We introduce EmoReward, a new self-evolving training mechanism that distills evidence reliability from reward traces collected during an actual training run to adaptively guide multi-reward weight allocation in subsequent training by determining which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. EmoReward first plans specific grounding cues from the emotional prompt to guide evaluation, then uses heterogeneous signal primitives to score the generated video during the act stage. Reflective Reward Gating calibrates their contributions through instance-level gates for phase, face confidence, conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over the active set to produce the sample's fused reward. RewardMemory then estimates each primitive's reliability from rollout scores and outcomes within each emotional regime in the finished training run, then fixes bounded multipliers that calibrate fusion weights in the next training run without updating reward models. Experiments on HunyuanVideo 1.5 show improvements across multiple RL algorithms and compare EmoReward with other agentic reward methods under SAGE-GRPO. Ablations and transfer experiments on SD 3.5 and FLUX further support adaptive reward calibration for visual generation.

title: StreamDuo: A Live Commentator and a Research Agent for Unseen Games

details.title: StreamDuo: A Live Commentator and a Research Agent for Unseen Games
details.abstract: 🎮 Can a live AI commentator handle a game it has never seen before? We introduce StreamDuo , a two-agent framework for cross-game streaming commentary. Instead of relying solely on memorized game knowledge, a live commentator selectively queries a frozen research agent that retrieves relevant information from game wikis, all while the stream continues. Our key contributions include: Information-gain-based querying to learn when external knowledge is actually needed. On-policy self-distillation to help the commentator use noisy retrieved information effectively. Cross-game evaluation on 10 unseen games after training on only Baldur's Gate 3. StreamDuo improves entity recall from 0.082 to 0.116 and reduces source-game knowledge leakage from 9.9% to 1.0% compared with the retrained Proact-VL baseline, while achieving stronger commentary timing and quality. We welcome feedback and discussions!

title: VA-TDM: A Unified View for Improving Few-Step Diffusion Models by Velocity Adversarial Distillation

details.title: VA-TDM: A Unified View for Improving Few-Step Diffusion Models by Velocity Adversarial Distillation
details.abstract: Few-step distillation seeks to make diffusion and flow models efficient without sacrificing generation quality. While score-based distribution matching methods provide a strong foundation, accurately tracking the student's evolving distribution across intermediate few-step transitions remains challenging: direct score estimation on perturbed intermediate outputs suffers from high variance, whereas clean-target denoising can estimate a different distribution from the one used to update the student. Building on a flow-matching perspective, we introduce Velocity Adversarial Distillation (VAD), a unified framework that constructs student velocity fields along the sampling process and uses a learned critic to turn student–teacher velocity discrepancies into generator feedback. VAD unifies score distillation, Fisher-based matching, and conditional moment matching along two axes (which field to match and how to update the generator).

title: SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding

details.title: SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding
details.abstract: Excited to share SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding! On-policy supervision does not have to wait for full-response rollouts. SpecOPD samples fresh draft branches at reference anchors in parallel, shares target-prefix computation, and supervises each branch on its own sampled history. An E2E-TV surrogate directly targets acceptance length. Algorithm–system co-design makes this work across full, sparse, and linear attention: tree masks, branch-consistent indexer groups, and indexed state replay preserve branch histories while reusing shared computation. Results: Up to 41.45% higher five-benchmark mean acceptance length than the original drafter. 16.09× supervised-token throughput over sequential-rollout OPD with the 27B target and DFlash V2 under native configurations, excluding offline reference preparation. Up to 3.56× decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding on the 27B target. We evaluate Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.8-27B, and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-125B with DFlash, DSpark, and DFlash V2 across dialogue, coding, math, and agentic workloads. The repository currently contains the project overview and figures; training code, evaluation scripts, and model weights are not included in the initial release. title: VidDub: Replacement-Aware Distillation for Two-Step Video Dubbing

details.title: VidDub: Replacement-Aware Distillation for Two-Step Video Dubbing
details.abstract: Video dubbing aims to synthesize lip movements that match target speech while preserving the speaker identity, head pose, and background of a source video. Existing editors are predominantly trained via self-reconstruction under original paired audio, even though the source mouth becomes a conflicting target when driving speech is replaced. We introduce replacement-aware cross-audio supervision: paired-audio samples use full-frame reconstruction, whereas unpaired replacement-audio samples mask out source-mouth reconstruction losses and supervise the mouth solely through audio-visual synchronization while preserving unmasked facial regions and background. Because offline dubbing provides the complete source video and target speech beforehand, we present VidDub, a full-context diffusion editor distilled into two denoising steps (2 NFE). Our replacement-aware teacher first learns accurate lip synchronization without regressing toward conflicting source mouth movements. Matched trajectory regression then transfers the teacher's CFG-guided trajectories to a two-step student, and distribution matching distillation recovers visual quality after step compression. We will release the curated training dataset, VidDub-Bench, fixed paired- and cross-audio evaluation manifests, preprocessing outputs, and unified evaluation code. Across three training seeds, masking out conflicting source-mouth reconstruction improves cross-audio Sync-C by 0.833; the final two-step model combines strong lip synchronization with superior visual quality, identity preservation, and visual speech recognition across four benchmarks.

title: LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers

details.title: LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers
details.abstract: Looped transformers reuse the same layers across loop steps, but every loop step stores its own KV cache, so memory grows with the loop count. LoopVQ exploits the redundancy of this cache along the loop axis: it vector-quantizes channels from several loop steps jointly with a single code and fine-tunes the codebooks to reflect each loop step’s sensitivity to quantization. → 0.25–0.5 bits per KV element (32–64× compression), near-BF16 accuracy on Ouro and Huginn, and up to 6.1× peak serving throughput for Ouro-2.6B on an RTX 6000 Ada GPU, with an SGLang + Triton implementation.

title: NitroFusion2: Bringing Adversarial Loss to the Text Stream of Multimodal Diffusion Transformers

details.title: NitroFusion2: Bringing Adversarial Loss to the Text Stream of Multimodal Diffusion Transformers
details.abstract: Hi, first author here. In an MMDiT, text and image tokens share every attention layer, so by mid-network the text tokens have already read the image. We use these intermediate text-token states of a frozen MMDiT as the discriminator's representation ( Text-Stream Adversarial Distillation ). In controlled ablations, text-stream discrimination outperforms conventional image-stream discrimination, and combining both streams is best on most metrics. Because the discriminator reads the text stream, its text condition also steers what it judges: swapping the cue (typography, objects, style, …) turns it into an expert on that aspect, with aspect-specific gains ( Aspect-Cued Discrimination ). Built on Z-Image-Turbo, NitroFusion2 brings few-step distillation from 4–8 steps down to 1–2 steps. Questions and feedback welcome! details.abstract: 🔊 LiveFoley: A Plug-and-Play Sound Engine for Real-Time Interactive Worlds Streaming Video-to-Audio (V2A) is notoriously hard. We tackle two major bottlenecks in current audio generation: ⚡️The Ultra-Low Latency Challenge: Unlike turn-based AI (e.g., GPT-Realtime), interactive V2A requires continuous, imperceptible latency. When a user knocks on a virtual table, the sound must trigger instantly. Both video encoding and audio synthesis must execute within a strict perceptual budget (<250ms). This constraint leaves prior streaming models lagging far behind offline models (like MMAudio). LiveFoley completely solves this visual frontend bottleneck using a novel Trailing Sliding Window, matching offline models in alignment with an end-to-end latency of just 156ms. 🎮 Versatile & Plug-and-Play (Beyond Joint Generation): The recent trend of joint video-audio world models tightly couples sound to their internal video generators, rendering them unusable for external visual streams. LiveFoley introduces a paradigm shift: it acts as a decoupled, source-agnostic sound engine. It synthesizes synchronized audio on-the-fly from any live pixel stream, making it instantly deployable for 3D game engines, AR/VR, and live cameras. A big step towards truly immersive interactive worlds!

title: Why Pay for Long Reasoning When Rewrite Do Trick? Causal Effects of Reasoning History Compaction on Future Generation and Agent Cost

details.title: Why Pay for Long Reasoning When Rewrite Do Trick? Causal Effects of Reasoning History Compaction on Future Generation and Agent Cost
details.abstract: ShortReasoning In ShortReasoning , I show that rewriting a model’s earlier reasoning into compact state can shorten its newly generated reasoning without retraining. In the coding-agent case study, MiniMax M3 with external compaction cost 34% less and used 59% less summed model-request time, including rewrite overhead. (all “frontier” open models from july 2026 were tested - DeepSeek, Nemotron, GLM, Kimi, MiniMax and all on average produce shorter reasoning) I built a simple compactor, but there is plenty anyone can play with: Which model compacts: a specialist fine-tune, a smaller cheaper model, or a fast “System 1”-style model. Classifiers could help select what to keep. What context it gets: one reasoning block, or more of the task and history? How much it compacts: individual blocks, many-to-many rewrites, or many-to-one summaries. How faithfully: aim to preserve information, as I did, or summarize only the most important parts. How inference is scheduled: run compression asynchronously alongside tool execution to potentially hide some rewrite latency. Broader takeaway Across all six tested routes, accepted compact histories led to shorter median continuations. My bet is that the capability is already there across most, perhaps all, current open-weight reasoning models. We should incentivize future generations to use it , expressing useful analysis in fewer tokens while keeping their problem-solving ability. This method can already generate compact traces for simple self-distillation . The compressor can be the model itself, or potentially a weaker model, since rewriting may be easier than solving the original task.

title: Harness-S: Learning from Sibling Harnesses for Generalizable Agent Training

details.title: Harness-S: Learning from Sibling Harnesses for Generalizable Agent Training
details.abstract: Harness evolution from a common base exhibits Locality, Complementarity, and Nonstationarity: variants repair different failures, and their utility changes as the policy learns. Rather than seeking a universally superior harness, we introduce Harness-S to selectively rescue failures of a base execution system through sibling harnesses and transfer the resulting capabilities into a single policy that remains effective under the original harness. Directional Harness Evolution develops specialized sibling harnesses along distinct repair directions, forming a reusable Sibling Harness Pool that remains fixed during policy training. Complementary Harness Rescue Training invokes this pool only when all initial attempts under the base harness fail. The same policy generates fresh rollouts under selected auxiliary harnesses, and these trajectories replace the failed group for reinforcement learning. An Adaptive Harness Router selects the Top-k variants using Harness Behavior Profiles and voting across multiple LLMs. Policy-aware profile re-anchoring refreshes this evidence as the policy learns. Across AppWorld, SWE-Gym, and DBBench, the trained policy substantially outperforms policy-only training when returned to the original base harness. Behavioral analyses and held-out cases support the transfer of harness-elicited behaviors into the policy itself. Reusing the router for Rank-1 inference provides additional gains at the same executor rollout count.

details.title: Random Is Almost Enough? Stable and Low-Cost Benchmark Compression via BestRand
details.abstract: Evaluating models on full benchmarks is often expensive. Benchmark compression reduces this cost by using small subsets to approximate full-benchmark results. This paper theoretically explains why random sampling works surprisingly well for benchmark compression but can be unstable, and introduces BestRand, a simple, stable, and low-cost solution. Across 70+ benchmarks, BestRand reduces high-error risk by 50.2% and estimation error by 16.4%, while requiring only 51.3% of the construction cost of competing methods.

title: EvoMemState: Evolving Memory State for Personal Agents

details.title: EvoMemState: Evolving Memory State for Personal Agents
details.abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to provide continuous personalized assistance by retaining user information across interactions. Existing systems support this process through fact extraction, organization, updating, and retrieval, but largely maintain memories as independent facts. This fact-centric paradigm may overlook how new facts update, constrain, or conflict with earlier ones, while leaving their applicability, role, and priority for the current request implicit. In this paper, we introduce EvoMemState, a state-centric framework that augments persistent facts with two complementary states: Relational States that capture how facts remain valid and relate to one another as memory evolves, and a Reasoning State that determines how these facts should be applied to the current request. Specifically, EVOMEMSTATE consists of three key components: (i) Ontology-Guided Memory State Induction extracts Persistent Facts and constructs Relational States that maintain their validity, scope, and evolving relations. (ii) RL-Based State Evolution internalizes memory-use experience into a policy through reinforcement learning to generate a request-specific Reasoning State. (iii) State-Aware Reasoning then combines the relevant facts with their Relational States and the generated Reasoning State to guide the personal agent. Extensive experiments on long-term dialogue and memory-use benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing memory systems in retrieval completeness and memory-grounded response accuracy. Our code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/EvoMemState.git .

title: VisSearch-Bench: Evaluating Long Horizon Visual Search in Multimodal Agents

details.title: VisSearch-Bench: Evaluating Long Horizon Visual Search in Multimodal Agents
details.abstract: VisSearch-Bench evaluates how multimodal agents organize and use visual evidence during long-horizon web search. It contains 204 human-written tasks across five search categories, spanning 7 domains and 25 subdomains. The tasks require agents to connect information across images, objects, and search steps to compare candidates, follow visual clues, and produce complete answers. Each task includes a reference answer, traceable evidence, and scoring rules. Evaluation measures both full task success and the correctness and completeness of individual results. Across 16 multimodal models, the best system fully solves only 26.47% of tasks, highlighting the challenge of managing visual context even with search tools.

title: Towards Foundation Decision Models: Drex

details.title: Towards Foundation Decision Models: Drex
details.abstract: We present Drex, a family of four open decision models that return a calibrated probability distribution over user-defined options in a single forward pass, without autoregressive decoding. Each request pairs a state (a document, record, or agent context, optionally with images) with questions asking for a choice, a yes/no judgment, or a score on an ordered scale. The family spans 8B (DLM), 9B (v1.5), 35B-A3B (v2.0), and 27B (Max) parameters. Training combines supervised fine-tuning with our in-house RL recipe, reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF), which blends verified outcomes with a reasoning judge under a KL constraint; ablations show RLAF raises accuracy while consistency losses cut option-order flips from 6.3% to 4.2%. Drex Max sets a new state of the art among decision models on Decision Index 0.4.1 (67.52 vs. 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0) and holds its score on maintainer-run private tests (66.60). On the independently run Artificial Analysis Decision Index, Max has the second-highest score among decision models, and Drex is among the most widely used decision models on OpenRouter. All weights and inference code are open: github.com/nace-ai/drex-decision-models

title: On the Opportunities and Challenges of Prefill-to-Autoregressive Cross-Model Transfer

details.title: On the Opportunities and Challenges of Prefill-to-Autoregressive Cross-Model Transfer
details.abstract: How much can a small model benefit from a larger model that only processes the prompt—and what actually drives the improvement? We explore these questions in this new paper. In prefill-to-autoregressive cross-model transfer (PACT), a larger sender processes the prompt and passes internal representations to a smaller receiver, which then generates the response independently. We introduce PLatour, a simple and scalable framework that connects frozen models through lightweight linear bridges trained directly with reinforcement learning. It also supports hybrid-attention architectures. On generation tasks, PLatour substantially outperforms the evaluated open-source PACT baselines. Using a 35B sender, it also exceeds Mostik AI’s reported results on shared math and coding benchmarks, compared with Mostik's 753B sender—although the training setups may differ. But stronger benchmark results do not, by themselves, establish useful information transfer. On some tasks, replacing sender representations with question-independent signals or training the receiver alone reproduces much of the improvement. Trainable bridges can provide substantial adaptation capacity even when both model backbones are frozen. The evidence is task-dependent: controls nearly match PLatour on GSM8K, while PLatour retains gains beyond all tested controls on Chemistry with chain-of-thought generation. To examine this systematically, we introduce PACT-Check. It combines interventions on sender information with separately trained adaptation baselines. PACT-Score measures the accuracy margin over the strongest applicable control. Our takeaway: PACT shows promising performance, but understanding its benefits requires distinguishing useful sender information from gains achievable through adaptation. We hope PLatour and PACT-Check help the community investigate when prefill-only communication helps—and how to make those benefits more reliable.

details.title: Open-HumanScale: An Open Recipe for Scaling Human and Robot Experience for Embodied Foundation Models
details.abstract: Hi everyone! We’re the authors of Open-HumanWAM , an open recipe for scaling human and robot experience for embodied foundation models. We study how human experience can improve robot learning, using Open-HumanWAM-50K , a 50,000-hour egocentric corpus with hand-motion and language annotations. 📈 HumanWAM-Vanilla — scaling human experience: our exploration studies show that scaling egocentric pretraining improves generalization to unseen scenes and randomized environments. Greater data diversity strengthens the scaling trend, while human pretraining improves robot demonstration efficiency. The final model achieves 92.08% Clean / 68.88% Random , averaging 80.48% on RoboTwin 2.0 . 🤖 HumanWAM-Goal — zero-shot transfer: combining human and robot experience improves zero-shot generalization in simulation and the real world. Visual goals enable robots to follow human demonstrations and adapt their behavior through in-context conditioning, without target-task parameter updates. 🏆 RoboTwin 2.0 Rank #1: after post-training, HumanWAM-Goal achieves 92.70% Clean / 84.60% Random , averaging 88.65% . title: HeLM: Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory for Non-Markovian Manipulation

details.title: HeLM: Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory for Non-Markovian Manipulation
details.abstract: 🤖 HeLM: Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory for Non-Markovian Manipulation How can robots track task progress when the current observation alone is insufficient? We introduce HeLM, a hierarchical VLM–VLA framework that maintains task-relevant history in explicit language memory. Two key aspects of our work: 🧠 Event-triggered memory updates: HeLM separates visual event detection from memory updates. The HLP updates memory and generates the next action command only when a task-relevant event is detected or the instruction changes. 🔄 Inter-episode memory: We introduce tasks where robots must remember information acquired under previous instructions, such as a human-demonstrated button sequence. We evaluate HeLM on 10 real-world non-Markovian tasks (56 variants) . Our two-stage inference improves average intra-episode subtask success from 67.7% to 85.7% compared with a one-stage variant. We also provide detailed failure analyses and evaluations of memory scalability. We welcome feedback and discussions on memory for robot learning!

title: Future Representation Distillation for Imagination-free World Action Models

details.title: Future Representation Distillation for Imagination-free World Action Models
details.abstract: Can we scale up imagination-free WAMs (e.g., Fast-WAM)? Excited to share DreamFree — an imagination-free WAM that improves with stronger video models and more video data, running at 11 Hz with a 14B video backbone. Video models learn how the world changes, providing useful knowledge for robot control. But generating future videos is costly, and prediction errors can affect actions. Imagination-free WAMs, e.g., Fast-WAM, enable robot control without generating future videos. But for Fast-WAM, stronger video priors don't automatically mean better control. In our experiments, scaling from 5B to 14B did not improve success. How can we make imagination-free WAMs benefit from stronger video models? Our key idea: turn the pretrained video model into a predictive visual encoder A frozen video teacher sees the future. The encoder learns to predict the teacher’s representation from the current view. This teaches the encoder to anticipate scene changes without generating future videos. Training the encoder needs only videos, without using action labels. Next, we train the action DiT using robot demonstrations with action labels. From the encoder’s visual representation, a readout learns to extract action-relevant information. An action decoder uses this information to predict robot actions. What we find: Real-world performance: Trained on DROID alone, DreamFree achieves 64% success across 10 real-world tasks, outperforming DreamZero at 56% and π0.5 at 16%. We evaluate the policies without task-specific fine-tuning. Fast inference: A 14B video backbone runs at 11 Hz on a single H200, with 17.8× faster inference than DreamZero. Memory efficiency: With a 14B video backbone, DreamFree fits on a single A6000 GPU with 48 GB of memory, without future-video generation or classifier-free guidance at inference. Better scaling: Scaling the video backbone from 5B to 14B significantly improves performance, enabling real-world manipulation on DROID and bimanual YAM. More video data further improves control without additional action labels. Video-only task transfer: DreamFree learns new task sequences from videos, including demonstrations from a different robot embodiment, without action labels for the new tasks.

title: SAE Interprets MoE: Sparse AutoEncoders Reveal That MoE Experts Exhibit Human-Interpretable Fine-Grained Specialization

details.title: SAE Interprets MoE: Sparse AutoEncoders Reveal That MoE Experts Exhibit Human-Interpretable Fine-Grained Specialization
details.abstract: TL;DR : We train a TopK SAE with 2^20 latents and k = 100 on the MoE block output of Qwen3-30B-A3B at layers 4, 30 and 46. Because the SAE encoder is affine and the MoE output is a weighted sum of expert outputs, the activation of each latent decomposes exactly over the activated experts. Aggregating this decomposition over 1.5B tokens gives every expert a dominant set of latents that it principally drives. This lets us read what each expert does without any predefined domain taxonomy. Key findings: Contribution is far more concentrated than gating. Most latents have only one or two dominators. Dominant sets are largely private to each expert. Experts specialize below coarse domains. A Java expert sits next to a separate expert for front end web code, and a geometry expert sits next to one for arithmetic and polynomials. Grouping the 128 experts of layer 30 gives 11 domains of very unequal size. Some domains are not subject areas at all, such as text form, language, and entities and identifiers. Code, the three SAEs, and an interactive explorer of all 128 experts of layer 30 are released. Happy to answer questions!

title: From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts: Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence

details.title: From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts: Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence
details.abstract: From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts: Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence For a decade, AI progress has been measured by how much a machine can do on its own. Agents now write code and run multistep tasks for us, yet people still forget what they once knew, miss what they are not looking at, and face hard choices without their own history. As AI moves into the physical world, attention has settled on one kind of intelligent individual, the embodied robot. This perspective paper argues that the era of Physical AI holds a second kind of equal importance: the person augmented by AI. What the paper covers: 🧠 AHI alongside AGI: AGI asks how intelligent a machine can be; AI-Augmented Human Intelligence (AHI) asks how much intelligence a machine can enable in a particular person. 🎧 The cognitive symbiont: a lifelong, embedded, real-time, private, low-friction, and proactive companion that senses what the person senses through external devices, keeps their context across years, and takes part in their thinking at the right moment. 📏 The cognitive gap: the conceptual core, the distance between what a person could bring to a situation and what they can hold in working memory. 🔄 The symbiosis loop: sensing, keeping, understanding, living alongside, acting for and thinking with the person, and growing, enclosed by a personal runtime and by trust. 🪜 A ladder of assistance: getting things done, thinking and feeling with the person, and living among others with the person, up to the meeting of two symbionts. ⚖️ Risk and governance: from covert assistance in examinations to pressure on everyone to adopt it, with 23 open problems and the conditions that would prove the paper wrong. 🌐 Project page: https://cognitive-symbiont.github.io Feedback and discussion are very welcome!

title: Decode Before You Hear: Speculative Listening for Chunk-Interleaved Full-Duplex Speech Language Models

details.title: Decode Before You Hear: Speculative Listening for Chunk-Interleaved Full-Duplex Speech Language Models
details.abstract: Decode Before You Hear: Speculative Listening for Full-Duplex Speech Language Models Most existing full-duplex speech models alternate between listening and speaking in fixed time chunks, which leaves the load across chunks highly uneven: compute sits idle during "listening", while "speaking" and tool calls miss their deadlines and fall behind because they generate many tokens serially. We observe that with silence as the hypothesized input, the output of 95.3% of chunks is identical to the output produced from the real audio, and 88% of divergences appear at the very first token. Building on this, Speculative Listening uses the idle compute of listening to draft the next chunk before the real audio arrives, using silence and the runner-up first-token candidate. All drafts are then verified together once the audio arrives, which requires no additional training and guarantees lossless output. Speed: On TickTock-Bench, the eight-task evaluation suite we built, speaking chunks are accelerated by 2.6–2.8×, and tool-call chunks by up to 23.4×. Latency: Decoding latency before a response begins drops by 73% on average, to 74–241 ms, close to the 200 ms turn-taking gap in human conversation. The maximum lag behind real time is reduced by 94.4%.

title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma

details.title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
details.abstract: Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal less about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient's condition throughout a course of care. To close this gap, we introduce NPCBench, a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). NPCBench mirrors specialist training, from guideline and foundational knowledge to case planning, longitudinal review, CarePath integration, and open-ended consultation. It contains 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. The episode-level evaluation tests whether diagnostic and care answers are jointly correct within a care pathway. By linking stepwise tasks to patient-level care trajectories, NPCBench evaluates whether models ground decisions in visual evidence, interpret changes in patient state, and meet clinical requirements in consultation. Across 30 evaluated models, we observe a composition gap: strong performance on individual tasks does not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, strict CarePath success reaches at most 23%. Paired controls and physician calibration further examine evidence grounding, longitudinal revision, and consultation judging. Overall, NPCBench broadens the evaluation of medical artificial intelligence beyond static question-answering paradigms to an apprenticeship-oriented assessment of clinical workflows, thereby offering a testbed for evidence-based and temporally coherent reasoning in oncology care.

title: SynthFaces: Balanced Large Scale Human Dataset

details.title: SynthFaces: Balanced Large Scale Human Dataset
details.abstract: Face datasets are heavily skewed across age, race and gender, and large real-world collections include people who never agreed to be used for training. We propose SynthFaces, a synthetic alternative that is balanced by design. A label-conditional flow matching model, ID-Flow, samples new identities for any chosen demographic group. An identity-conditioned generator turns them into face images, which are then placed into varied, captioned scenes. The result is a large dataset of non-existent people, with about 10 images per identity. It can be used to train and fine-tune fairer identity-preserving models without real personal data. Accepted to BMVC 2026.

title: Decoupled Predictive Decision Making: A Shared Conditional Predictor for Agents

details.title: Decoupled Predictive Decision Making: A Shared Conditional Predictor for Agents
details.abstract: We introduce Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM) , an architecture that turns historical experience into predictions for agent decisions through a shared pretrained learner. The key idea is to separate semantic representation from empirical inference. An LLM represents current and historical records, while a conditional predictor uses the represented evidence to predict task-defined targets. This brings together two complementary capabilities: semantic knowledge from language pretraining and empirical inference from structured-data pretraining. Tool judgments, candidate preferences, and reasoning assessments share the same evidence-and-query interface, with predictions converted into choices by a decision rule. We use a single frozen LimiX-2 predictor across all five evaluated task categories, without updating either model’s neural parameters at deployment. Key results: Across 50 benchmarks: With Qwen3.5-27B as the semantic encoder, mean accuracy rises from 78.80% with few-shot prompting to 84.92% with DPDM at the methods’ respective evaluated history budgets. With identical histories and queries, DPDM reaches 82.33% . Tool-use assessment: On ToolPRMBench’s BFCL and ToolSandbox tasks, accuracy improves over few-shot prompting by 34.26 and 28.87 percentage points , respectively, at the methods’ respective evaluated history budgets. Accuracy also improves as history grows. Imbalanced histories: With identical imbalanced histories, DPDM improves mean balanced accuracy over few-shot prompting by 14.51 percentage points across five reasoning-step assessment tasks and four encoders. DPDM makes learning from experience an independently improvable foundation-model capability: advances in a shared conditional predictor can improve decisions across agent tasks. We welcome feedback and discussion!

title: Harness-S: Learning from Sibling Harnesses for Generalizable Agent Training

details.title: Harness-S: Learning from Sibling Harnesses for Generalizable Agent Training
details.abstract: Harness evolution from a common base exhibits Locality, Complementarity, and Nonstationarity: variants repair different failures, and their utility changes as the policy learns. Rather than seeking a universally superior harness, we introduce Harness-S to selectively rescue failures of a base execution system through sibling harnesses and transfer the resulting capabilities into a single policy that remains effective under the original harness. Directional Harness Evolution develops specialized sibling harnesses along distinct repair directions, forming a reusable Sibling Harness Pool that remains fixed during policy training. Complementary Harness Rescue Training invokes this pool only when all initial attempts under the base harness fail. The same policy generates fresh rollouts under selected auxiliary harnesses, and these trajectories replace the failed group for reinforcement learning. An Adaptive Harness Router selects the Top-k variants using Harness Behavior Profiles and voting across multiple LLMs. Policy-aware profile re-anchoring refreshes this evidence as the policy learns. Across AppWorld, SWE-Gym, and DBBench, the trained policy substantially outperforms policy-only training when returned to the original base harness. Behavioral analyses and held-out cases support the transfer of harness-elicited behaviors into the policy itself. Reusing the router for Rank-1 inference provides additional gains at the same executor rollout count.

title: On the Opportunities and Challenges of Prefill-to-Autoregressive Cross-Model Transfer

details.title: On the Opportunities and Challenges of Prefill-to-Autoregressive Cross-Model Transfer
details.abstract: How much can a small model benefit from a larger model that only processes the prompt—and what actually drives the improvement? We explore these questions in this new paper. In prefill-to-autoregressive cross-model transfer (PACT), a larger sender processes the prompt and passes internal representations to a smaller receiver, which then generates the response independently. We introduce PLatour, a simple and scalable framework that connects frozen models through lightweight linear bridges trained directly with reinforcement learning. It also supports hybrid-attention architectures. On generation tasks, PLatour substantially outperforms the evaluated open-source PACT baselines. Using a 35B sender, it also exceeds Mostik AI’s reported results on shared math and coding benchmarks, compared with Mostik's 753B sender—although the training setups may differ. But stronger benchmark results do not, by themselves, establish useful information transfer. On some tasks, replacing sender representations with question-independent signals or training the receiver alone reproduces much of the improvement. Trainable bridges can provide substantial adaptation capacity even when both model backbones are frozen. The evidence is task-dependent: controls nearly match PLatour on GSM8K, while PLatour retains gains beyond all tested controls on Chemistry with chain-of-thought generation. To examine this systematically, we introduce PACT-Check. It combines interventions on sender information with separately trained adaptation baselines. PACT-Score measures the accuracy margin over the strongest applicable control. Our takeaway: PACT shows promising performance, but understanding its benefits requires distinguishing useful sender information from gains achievable through adaptation. We hope PLatour and PACT-Check help the community investigate when prefill-only communication helps—and how to make those benefits more reliable.
